PRIVILEGE-MR. HARRIS ORDER FOR RETURN SHOWING PURCHASES OF LAND IN PICKERING TOWNSHIP
speechtext:
I rise to a question of privilege. On February 24 last an order was passed for a return answering the following questions:
1.	Has the government bought land in Pickering township, Ontario county, during the last two years?
2.	If so, how many acres?
3.	For what purpose is the land to be used?
The return has been duly filed, but it is incomplete. To use a common expression, it sidesteps the question entirely, in that the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) brought down a long tabulated report of expenditures being made in Pickering township. Through his department lands have been bought or expropriated, at any rate they have been entered upon; fences have been taken down, and at present there is work going on on these particular lands in that county on account of the department.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. HARRIS ORDER FOR RETURN SHOWING PURCHASES OF LAND IN PICKERING TOWNSHIP
speechtext: What does the return say?

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. HARRIS ORDER FOR RETURN SHOWING PURCHASES OF LAND IN PICKERING TOWNSHIP
speechtext:
The return
says nothing-that is my complaint, and that is why I am raising the question of privilege. Surely an hon. member is entitled to have a proper return rather than a nebulous one of this kind. The return goes on to say that the Department of Justice has not bought any land, the Secretary of State has not bought any land, and so on and so on.
I make one further observation. Immediately that question is put on the order paper, before the printer's ink is dry, the minister's department knows all about it; they are just like watchdogs, knowing everything that happens -and quite rightly so; but to my mind there is an utter lack of frankness in imparting information to hon. members of this house when it is asked for in a straightforward way.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND REVIEW REGULATIONS AND NATURALIZATION AND DEPORTATION LAW'S

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, March 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King for the appointment of a committee to consider and review the defence of Canada regulations passed under the War Measures Act, and the naturalization and deportation laws.
Mrs. DORISE W. NIELSEN (North Battle-ford) : Mr. Speaker, I am very glad indeed that the debate was adjourned last evening in order that other lion, members might have the opportunity to take part in it. During last session some of us thought hon. members should have been given greater opportunity to express their opinions with regard to the defence of Canada regulations. Since we have that opportunity now I feel that each of us should make the most of it and discuss all these regulations very thoroughly and from every angle and every aspect. I certainly hope the debate will not be closed before more hon. members have taken advantage of this chance to express their opinions, because I believe the country itself is very anxious to know more of what hon. members of this house think with regard to the regulations. I also hope that in particular hon. members on the government benches will take part in the debate, because it is far better to speak and risk being a goat than to say nothing and be a sheep.
Theoretically I am in agreement that there is a need for protection in this country not only against the ideology but against the spreading of the ideas of fascism in any oractical manner, because we as a nation undoubtedly are fighting the spreading of that ideology among our own people, who are democratic. I feel that we are in disagreement with the ideas of fascism, which call for the supremacy of the state and so on. We must remain opposed to them, and we must do everything possible to prevent the spread of those ideas among our own people. But I do not agree that in practice these regulations are having just that effect. In some instances, of course, we have had the arrest of people supposed to be fascists, but I feel that in other cases under these regulations we have done just the contrary. Just recently I have noticed two formulations; perhaps they may be accidental, but I happened to 14873-77*
notice them. One appears in a little pamphlet which I believe has been mentioned in this house previously, published under the direction of the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Gardiner) and called "The Two Ways of Life." In the introduction I notice this statement:
Our way of life is the civilized way of life. It is the civilized way because under it every citizen enjoys the right to worship as he please-
That is correct. Then it goes on to say:
-to select his own rulers, to help make his own laws-
And so on. Then I notice that, speaking on February 24, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is reported in Hansard as having said:
In a democracy the designation of the rulers of those who are to be governed is and must be made by the vote of the people.
I do not like that word "rulers"; I intensely dislike the idea. Perhaps this idea of the government being the ruler of the people comes from the fact that within the last year this government has taken to itself unusual and enormous power. We are fighting against the idea of the supremacy of the state over the individual. We are fighting against the idea of rulers over the people. We who are democratic must always insist that the duly elected representatives of the people maintain the status of servants of the people, not their rulers.
I notice also, very happily, that on February 27 the Minister of Justice assured this assembly that the defence of Canada regulations would last only for the duration of the war. According to Hansard the minister said:
They are operative in a state of emergency, and they will disappear as soon as we have peace and victory, as we hope to have some day.
I believe the minister was very honest and sincere when he made that statement; I have no reason to believe that he would be otherwise. Yet I would suggest that the Minister of Justice of to-day may not be minister of justice when this war is over. He may be retired; he may be in another office; we may have another minister of justice who is not of the same mind. The people of this nation have no other guarantee, so far as I know, than a statement by our present Minister of Justice, that these defence of Canada regulations will disappear as soon as the war is over. I do not know myself whether we should be willing to accept such a flimsy guarantee. We have no legislation upon which we can rely.
During the time of the trial of the seaman Sullivan, I believe it was, Mr. Justice Hope said that during war time we people of Canada
1204	COMMONS
Defence of Canada-Special Committee
should be willing to put our civil rights and liberties in pawn. I must confess I do not know very much about pawnshops. I have always said that in northern Saskatchewan we have not had many social services, and this was one we did not have-the pawnshops. And I think perhaps in the past I might have been pleased to avail myself of that service. Now, when an article of any value is placed in pawn, a ticket is given in exchange, and through that ticket the borrower may redeem the article of value. Where is that ticket the Canadian people should have to-day, with which they may retrieve their freedom and certain of their rights and liberties which under these defence of Canada regulations are being taken from them?
Several hon. members have said on different occasions in the house that the government has a mandate from the people. Would it perhaps not be wiser to say "has had"? We live in a time of swiftly moving events, let us never forget that. During the last year events have moved very swiftly, possibly more swiftly than at any other time in our history. People who a year ago viewed certain things with a measure of complacency to-day view with alarm and with growing apprehension the tide of affairs within our country.
During the last year we have seen the application of the defence of Canada regulations, of which at the time of the election we had not become aware to any great extent. We have seen numbers-I do not know exactly how many-of our ordinary citizens interned without, as I say, the usual process of law and guarantee of trial. We have seen certain groups in this country called illegal. We have seen certain measures of compulsion with regard to the war effort. Undoubtedly there is in Canada to-day a certain amount of compulsion upon people who are working in factories or in various businesses in connection with the war savings campaign. Undoubtedly -and I do not believe this can be denied- unequal sacrifices are being made in this war. During the last year we have witnessed an enormous spending programme and the creation of a vast debt, a debt greater and more stupendous than the people of this nation have ever had to accept before. We have seen a serious situation in western Canada, one which so far seems almost impossible of solution; this government apparently has no solution to offer. We have seen rule by order in council. That, again, is a dictatorial and not a democratic procedure. We have seen various orders in council directed against organized labour in Canada.
I say now emphatically that many Canadians, who a year ago viewed these regulations
rMra. Nielsen.]
with more or less complacency and were willing to leave them in the hands of the government, are to-day viewing them with apprehension. The regulations have not the support of the people. I say without hesitation that among many groups of people there is the growing belief that these defence of Canada regulations are being used deliberately to stifle the apprehensions of the people and the expression of their apprehension and discontent. The government is trying to silence the protests of the people. It is asking for unity, but it is trying to enforce unity of opinion. The fact that the government is using these regulations to enforce conformity of opinion is, in the view of some of us, an indication that it is well aware that the people are not unanimous in their agreement with the policy of the government and the legislation it has enacted. Moreover, I would go so far as to say that the very fact that the government is forced to put certain of these regulations into operation is an indication that it fears the expression of the people's will. There is growing discontent, and yet the government does little or nothing to eliminate the causes of discontent among our people. Rather it seeks to suppress the discontent by arbitrary rulings under these regulations. It acts as the ruler of the people, not as their servant.
Already we have heard a great deal about Mr. Meighen, and what he is reported to have said some time ago. At least he was honest. In effect he said that if an unregulated and unrestricted profits system were to be finished by this war, then he did not see what there was to fight for. I believe if any ordinary person, a member of a farmers' organization or a trade union, or a member of a relief recipients' association, had stated publicly that he did not see what there was to fight for, he would be in an internment camp cooling his heels. I believe I am safe in saying, however, that the government has at no time even thought of arresting Mr. Meighen. For one thing, the government does not fear the loss of Mr. Meighen's support, or the support of people like Mr. Meighen, and those he represents. The government can take that position because it is doing nothing, and does not intend to do anything, to limit or to restrict povrer, privilege or the profits system in Canada. In a time of war it is allowing-and there is not a shadow of doubt about it-a condition of profitable patriotism. We see, too, how clear it is that they need not fear people like Mr. Meighen, because legislation passed in the house and orders in council have declared protected areas for certain industries owned and controlled by monopolies in this country. We find that as an advisory com-

Defence of Canada-Special Committee
mittee the government has brought in business executives of some of the greatest monopolies and corporations in the country.
We know there has been no endeavour to conscript wealth. We are continuing to pay the interest on the loans we make from the great banks. All these things assure people like Mr. Meighen and his representatives that there is nothing to worry about. Therefore this government does not fear any expressions by Mr. Meighen. Well, that is all right. It is quite all right for Mr. Meighen to express himself in that way. But if Mr. Meighen is free so to express himself, then let us all be free to express our opinions.
It has been stated that roughly from one-third to one-half of all the people in Canada are earning less than $1,000 a year. Among that group of low-income people a certain amount of opinion is being expressed, not openly at public dinners, as Mr. Meighen is able to express himself, but among themselves. The people are saying many things. Some of them are saying: "If we are going to have conscription, conscription not only by legislation but by economic pressure, instead of being permitted freely to support the war effort; if we are to have compulsory saving introduced into this country; if our farmers are to be the neglected people and to suffer unduly from the burden of this war through no fault of their own but from loss of markets; if we are to be taxed so that we cannot even maintain health and strength in our families while corporations and monopolies are making greater profits during this time; if the banks are to get enormous interest, thereby hanging a burden of debt over our children in the years to come greater than we have had before, and if we are to lose our civil rights and to have no guarantee that they will be returned to us," is it any wonder that they say, "we can hardly see what we are fighting for?"
But the government does fear expression of these opinions. It does not intend to allow opinions of this kind to have expression because the government intends to continue the things about which the people would like to express their opinions adversely. It is clear that the government does intend to tax the low income groups. It is encouraging compulsory saving and it is allowing interest on debts to accumulate. It is not enforcing by legislation equality of sacrifice. By various orders in council it is impeding the trade union movement in this country. It has offered no constructive policy to agriculture. The government knows that as long as it conducts this war there will be a greater number of Canadian people who will want
to express themselves as being against the government policy. Therefore I have no hesitation in saying that these regulations are being used to suppress the free expression of the people's will.
With regard to my own pamphlets, I have very little to say. I have noticed that various hon. members of this house have been a little interested, maybe a little amused over these pamphlets. Personally I have not thought a great deal about the matter. In fact the government has never intimated to me in any way, shape or form why they did what they did. I have formed my own opinion about why that action was taken, I regard the -thing which the government did as being somewhat of a little blunder on their part. I refer to the taking of the pamphlets by 'the police. I think that was done deliberately in an attempt to intimidate not only me but the rest of the people of this country who were interested enough to want to read what a member of this house had said. After all is said and done, the best laid schemes of mice and men and governments gang aft agley. The attempted intimidation was not successful. In fact I feel I should thank the government for some good advertising.
In return I may say that I have done my best to advertise the government's little pamphlet. All hon. members know it. On various occasions I have spoken to the people of Canada about this twenty-five cents' worth of good information and told them that they should read it. But I have also told them that if these regulations are not amended to protect in essence the people of this country from the things from which they should be protected, the new edition should have across its front a different title; it should be called, "Defence of Capital Regulations."
There has -also been intimidation of our working people. Theoretically this may not have been intended, but in practice it has taken place. I believe certain members of the trade union movement have been arrested. The other day the Minister of Justice said that they had been arrested because they were communists. Not long ago I came across a copy of an address which had been made by the lawyer who defended Pat Sullivan of the seamen's union. This speech was delivered to the Civil Liberties association, of Toronto, at Emmanuel college, university of Toronto on November 1, 1940. This lawyer bad had access to fai more material than had bon. members of this house or the general public. I should
1206	COMMONS
Defence of Canada-Special Committee
like to quote briefly a few of the things he said about the arrest and internment of these trade union leaders. I quote:
Is the existence of regulation 21, administered by the policy, illustrated in the Sullivan case, of denying the detained person any particulars of the things held against him, forcing the accused to assume the onus of accusation and proof without knowing what he is expected to establish or refute, designed to assist our social effort at this moment? Does it rather encourage at least suspicion that the use of this arbitrary power may be associated, at least in part, with class or economic or political interests?
Let us examine two or three of the cases and see how they work out in actual result. Let us take the Sullivan case again to begin with.
Sullivan's arrest took place in June, just as the seamen's conciliation board was emerging from the first stage of its public sessions and was about to enter into private conference with the officers of the union and with representatives of the major companies for the purpose of trying to effect an agreement between the parties.
In point of time Sullivan's arrest seemed to fit in with the particular interests at the moment of the employers. The Department of Justice asserts that this was "the long arm of coincidence." I, personally, accept this assurance in good faith. But I am not a seaman, relying upon the union and the aid of its executive officers for concrete results in the matter of my livelihood. If I were, and found myself directly and injuriously affected by Sullivan's arrest just as he is to step up to bat for the winning run, I might feel differently. So might you, if you were such a seaman.
Again he goes on to say:
Let us take the case of one David Sinclair, also connected with the seamen's union. Sinclair was editor of the union's paper. He appeared with executive officers of the union at some of the conciliation board's hearings. He was arrested in Montreal, taken into detention under order of the Minister of Justice and sent to an internment camp early in the month of September. The grounds disclosed in his case are merely that representations have been made that he is (a) a member of the communist party, (b) a communist agitator.
A day or two before Sinclair's arrest, ballots had been counted in the Department of Labour at Ottawa of seamen employed in one fleet of shipping vessels, some 38 or so vessels in number, as a result of a vote ordered by the conciliation board, to determine whether or not these men desired to be represented by the union. The company had insisted that the men had no such desire. The result of the vote was that some 95 per cent or 97 per cent voted in favour of union representation-this, incidentally, several months after Sullivan's arrest and detention.
On the day before Sinclair's arrest he filed with the_ Canadian Press in Montreal, as publicity director for the union, a statement announcing the result of the vote, which would be followed by negotiations with the company for an agreement. The press announcement did not appear the next day, but neither did Sinclair.
There are probably as good reasons for the non-appearance of one as for the disappearance
[Mrs. Nielsen.1
of the other, and reasons quite independent each of the other. I do not know them. You do not know them. The seamen and their friends do not know them. The advisory committee will, but Sinclair and his counsel, so far, do not and probably will not. What conclusions, however erroneous, would you arrive at if you were a seaman or the friend of one?
If only these people were given the right of trial where truth could be brought forward there would not be the feeling of suspicion which exists in the minds of our people that these arbitrary regulations are being used in certain cases, not in favour of the people but rather in favour of a group in this country which has power and affluence.
Considering again other minority groups, one might mention the case of the Ukrainian people, the Ukrainian labour temple association. That group of people have carried on in this country a marvellous work. They brought with them from Europe some of their handicrafts and their dances. Their musical festivals have been one of the finest things they have been able to give to this country. I heard one time the cultural work of this Ukrainian group described as "an oasis of beauty in the arid desert of Canadian culture." And yet to-day that group is declared illegal t About a hundred of their buildings scattered across this country, built by themselves, by poor working people with their nickels and their dimes, have been taken over by the custodian of enemy alien property. These people are not enemy aliens. They are Canadian citizens, some of the finest we have in this country. How can you expect unity when you treat a minority group in such a way? For years they have been fighting against fascism and fascist tendencies, not only in Germany and Italy, but wherever they show themselves, and they have some experience from the past to guide them. These people have some of their property to-day in some cities rented to another organization which right up until before the beginning of this war was openly in support of Hitler. How these things must hurt! This government is asking for unity amongst all our people while at the same time it is doing the very things under the defence of Canada regulations which must absolutely preclude the possibility of unanimous support.
Again there is the Canadian Tribune, a paper which has been mentioned in this house before. I feel sure, and I repeat, that in the suspension of this paper there is a desire to intimidate those who have been reading it by trying to make them believe that the paper itself is a subversive organ. The Secretary

Defence of Canada-Special Committee
of State (Mr. Casgrain) when he mentioned this paper said to the house-I quote from Hansard of February 27 of this year:
I have in my hand one of the last issues of this newspaper, dated February 1, 1941. 1 need not read it to the house, but it contains references to certain speeches and utterances of a member of the British House of Commons.
How terrible! Fancy any Canadian paper publishing a speech made by a member of the British House of Commons! What an excuse! Of course I know that the minister went on to say he thought this paper was subversive because it was promoting the ideas of the communist party. But hon. members who are conversant with the rise of fascism in Italy, in Germany, and more recently still with that terrible arising of fascism in France, will know that those who had the power used the same old Red bogy. They brought it out of the cupboard to scare the people. The Red bogy-that was the thing that mattered. As long as the Red bogy was there the people would be afraid to do anything but what the people in power wanted. In Italy and in Germany this Red bogy was brought out to scare and intimidate the people, and here in Canada you- find the same thing happening. In France recently by arbitrary decree we saw, because of this Red menace which was supposed to be there, the imprisonment of thousands of French people. There may have been a proportion of communists among them, but there must also have been hundreds who were simply the leaders of the working people, in their farmers' groups, trade union groups and others, men and women -who had been fighting fascism. But they too were imprisoned-the very people who if they had had their freedom would have defended France to the very last ditch. But they were imprisoned, and it was the government, and big business control behind the government, which imprisoned them and then turned around and betrayed France into the hands of Hitler.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND REVIEW REGULATIONS AND NATURALIZATION AND DEPORTATION LAW'S
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND REVIEW REGULATIONS AND NATURALIZATION AND DEPORTATION LAW'S
speechtext:
No, I will permit a
question afterwards but I have not very much time left.
We have the same kind of thing beginning to spread in this country. Attempts are being made to scare us. Reference was made a while ago to an article by Commissioner Wood in which he stressed the Red menace. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members, there is far more need for us to fear that the powers that be in this country are not under the proper supervision of the people but are allowed, at the expense of the people, to
dictate to this government, whose profitable patriotism may lead this country into very severe and very terrible consequences.
I would urge that this committee which is to be set up consider in great detail the few things which have been brought to its notice and do what is possible to amend such of these regulations as restrict the expression of view of the people.
When the minister was mentioning the Canadian Tribune there was one thing to which he took exception, and that was that the Canadian Tribune gave some publicity to a large conference of the British working people which was held in England, in January of this year I believe. The Daily Minor, one of the large newspapers of England, described the people who went to that conference as ninety per cent honest-to-God British citizens. If we in this country have not the right to know what honest-to-God British citizens are saying, well, I think perhaps we have not the right to call ourselves a democracy. I have every reason to believe that there is in this country a large body of thought which perhaps I might call honest-to-God Canadian thought, far removed from the reds, and which to-day is seriously criticizing -these arbitrary regulations. The Canadian Tribune, although its circulation was not so great, might have linked up this feeling of -the people from the east to the west of Canada. It might have helped to organize the protest of these honest-to-God citizens of Canada against this government, and that is possibly one reason why the Canadian Tribune has been suspended, I see no reason why we should neglect to consider these things in their various -aspects.
In war time there is always a certain amount of hysteria which is purposely spread among the people to keep up their enthusiasm, and I know that there are many people in Canada today, and possibly some members of this house, of whom it might quite easily be said that under the pressure of war hysteria they are more or less prepared to let the government go ahead and do as it will. But I would say to you that in times like these we have every reason to think deeply and to think well. We must not let ourselves be carried away by emotional appeals. The British working man has a little saying which will perhaps give you some idea of what he means. Of course the British working man is not very careful of his language -and I hope, Mr. Speaker, you will excuse me for repeating it. The British working man says: "You must never let y-our bleeding heart run away with your bloody head." I feel that many people to-day under the influence of war hysteria are allowing themselves to be
1208	COMMONS
Defence of Canada-Special Committee
carried away. They are not looking at these regulations and observing their effect upon our people. If these regulations continue as they are now, where is the right of the ordinary citizens to express themselves, the right of the ordinary citizens to defend themselves against what they believe to be injustice? If these regulations continue in their present form I for one feel that this government will no longer have any right to call itself a democratic government of the Canadian people.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND REVIEW REGULATIONS AND NATURALIZATION AND DEPORTATION LAW'S
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the course of the debate on this resolution reference has been made to the suppression of certain newspapers and pamphlets on the ground that they were subversive of Canada's war effort. In speaking to the resolution I wish to refer to a newspaper or pamphlet which, while I do not go so far as to say it is subversive of Canada's war effort, is, I do say, subversive of national unity in Canada. I refer to a pamphlet or paper entitled "The Gospel Witness," edited by the Reverend T. T. Shields who, I understand, is pastor of a church in the city of Toronto.
I do not know how I come to be favoured with the receipt of these copies, except that, the contents of it being of a very insulting nature to the Catholic faith and the members of that church, the reverend gentleman thought he was privileged to add injury to insult and forward copies to the Catholic members.
It would take me all afternoon to read all the articles contained in these several copies that I have before me, with their insulting references to the Catholic church and its members. I will not take up the time of the house except to give one or two excerpts so that hon. members will have some conception of what is contained in this sheet, published by a clergyman belonging to a religious denomination which I respect, as I respect the members of every denomination throughout this country. That respect which I give to the members of other denominations and to the religious belief of every other, I expect to be given to mine. Consequently it is not in anger but rather in sorrow that I shall give these excerpts.
In the issue of this journal of January 2, 1941, there is an extract from a sermon preached in Jarvis street Baptist church, Toronto, on Sunday evening, December 29, 1940. One clause reads:
So is it of that religion which makes a man only a part of a great church. That is Roman Catholicism. Roman Catholicism is religious totalitarianism. Salvation is in the church. Everything is to be sacrificed for the church:

the individual does not count. That is not Christian; and that view, whether applied to the state or to religion, is essentially pagan and anti-Christian.
In another issue the same gentleman, this time giving a title to his sermon-"The Protestant Samson and the Papal Delilah"-[DOT] writes:
I shall never advocate any degree of appeasement anywhere at any time with popery. It is a religious racket, an organization which exists to make merchandise of the souls of men. The more I know of it the more I am driven to the conclusion that its officers must either be suffering from some terrible delusion or otherwise they must be outright knaves. It seems impossible to me to believe that any reasonable man can seriously believe the burlesque of Christianity that calls itself Roman Catholicism.
I know how vicious it can be. I know very well that its agents sometimes reckon they are doing God service when they actually kill. The bloody history of the Roman church proclaims that fact.
Speaking in this house as a humble member of that church, and, I believe, speaking in the names of four million Roman Catholics throughout this country, I protest with all the vigour of my manhood against the publication and circulation of such material. Thus the reverend gentleman throws his gratuitous insults into the faces of the Catholic population of this country. This is his conception of his duty as a religious leader to preach the doctrines of unity amongst all classes and creeds who so ardently desire the unity of our people during the most critical period in the history of our country.
I should like to ask the members of this house and the people of the country whether, in their opinion, such expressions and statements as I have just cited tend to bring about the unity which we so strongly desire in Canada in this most critical time of our history. It is not for me to pass judgment upon the reverend gentleman, but I would respectfully remind him of the words of the Master: "A new commandment I give unto you, that you love one another." I would ask that he respect this commandment and preach this doctrine of love instead of hatred.

Yet even that has been held up to ridicule by this distinguished clergyman in the city of Toronto. Nothing that can be done from the Catholic point of view but must be criticized and held up to ridicule. And we, numerous body that we are in this country, are supposed to do like the ostrich, hide our heads in the sand and take this abuse from him.
In sermons and speeches of this kind it is also the habit and the custom to speak of

It would seem to me that this question has been before this house on divers occasions, speeches were made reflecting on Quebec's loyalty and answers given thereto; and the answer made was clear and distinct enough. If to-day from the flagstaff of these buildings there flies the union jack it is because on two historic occasions the French-Canadian population of the province of Quebec stood loyally by and saved Canada for the British empire. Nevertheless the old bogy of French Canadian disloyalty must be trotted out to serve the purpose of selfish individuals.
Again this distinguished gentleman, in an article appearing in the same paper, entitled "The Religious Aspects of the Sirois Report," writes as follows:
But the indisputable fact is that the Roman Catholic church, like a malignant parasite, has fastened itself upon the body of Quebec and is draining it of the last drop of its blood, reducing it to something little better than an emaciated political skeleton, if the report is to be believed.
That is, the Sirois report.
And then this same malignant parasite stretches out its tentacles, and through a "handful of French Canadians led by Mr. Ernest Lapointe" seeks to wrap itself about the vitals of the whole dominion-including this province.
And on what grounds does Quebec demand these exceptional favours? Her superior loyalty? Her unusual service in peace or in war? The report tells us she was against us in the last war, and implies she is against us in this. The report tells us she was against ns in the last war on religious grounds: on the same grounds she is against us in this. Our position is that we are not opposed to the war savings certificates so long as only people who can afford to contribute are asked to subscribe, and so long as no one is coerced. In order to show what I mean in that regard, I should like to quote about half a dozen lines from an editorial which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of February 26:
An elderly woman in Regina, Saskatchewan, last week signed a pledge to purchase one war savings certificate every month. Her income is $20 a month, a sum she receives on a pension. To the canvasser who supplied the pledge form she said she could buy one certificate each month by doing without one meal each day.
We can admire that kind of sacrifice, but it is the sort of sacrifice that is not doing anyone any good. It is only when pressure is brought to bear to get such people to subscribe, that we are opposed to this war savings campaign. Mr. Speaker, this resolution provides for the setting up of a committee to consider the defence of Canada regulations and the law relating to naturalization. The qualifications for naturalization in Canada are not as strict and exacting as they should be. They require at least a year's residence in Canada with the previous four years in the British empire. The applicant for naturalization is supposed to have an adequate knowledge of the English or French language, but it is not necessary that he should be able to read or write. I suppose he must be a decent man, have no record of crime, and so on. It is a great privilege to become a naturalized citizen of Canada and a subject of the British empire. The qualifications should be more than an adequate knowledge of English or French. There should be some way of finding out whether an applicant recognizes the responsibilities involved in becoming a British subject and a Canadian citizen. He ought to know something of the history of this country and of how the benefits which he is obtaining have been won and handed down, of how hard it has been for the people of the British empire to obtain the privileges they enjoy to-day. He should be willing to accept and should be impressed by the necessity of accepting the obligation which goes with the privilege of becoming a British subject. If he has not got that thoroughly in his mind, there should be some way of educating him so that he will recognize that obligation fully. We do not want people to become naturalized British subjects or Canadian citizens simply for the benefits they are going to get out of naturalization. That reminds me of the man who was seeking naturalization in one province and, when asked by the judge why he wanted to become naturalized, said that he wanted to get a game licence. Naturally his application was turned down, but undoubtedly there are people who want to become British subjects for the privileges that go with our citizenship, and who do not want to accept the responsibilities of the citizenship which they assume.
Another thing. I think more instruction should be given in the schools in the history of the fight for the rights which go with citizenship in the British empire and Canadian citizenship. If more instruction were given along this line the fathers and mothers of the children who are attending school to-day would realize better the obligations and privileges of Canadian citizenship.
I feel strongly-this has been mentioned before but I think it will bear repeating-that naturalization should be more of an impressive ceremony that it now is. The applicant should not simply have to go into some back office, stand up and raise his right hand and
1214	COMMONS
Defence of Canada-Special Committee
say " I swear," and that be the end of it. Naturalization should take place in the form of a ceremony which would impress the candidate and make him realize that he is assuming the obligations of citizenship. Not enough of them do recognize that, although they recognize clearly the benefits which they are obtaining.
Just a word with respect to the defence of Canada regulations. I have in my riding in Toronto, and there are also in the adjoining riding and in fact all over Toronto, a great many new Canadians. They are fine citizens. There are, I suppose, in Canada altogther some 2,000,000 new Canadians of foreign birth or descent. Not the slightest shadow of doubt should be cast on the loyalty of these new Canadians as a group, because as a class they are just as loyal as any other class of Canadians. They have been the first fighters against subversive influences in their own groups. They have been the first to recognize the danger, they have fought it, and in some cases their blood has been spilled in the fight against subversive elements in their own groups. I know how loyal are the new Canadians in my riding and in the adjoining ridings, and I must say that they resent not being used to a greater extent than they are as guards and other work of the kind. We should extend the hand of friendship to them wherever we can and do our best to make them feel that they are not outsiders.
It has been suggested that there should be a three-man tribunal to hear appeals from those interned under the defence of Canada regulations. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has suggested that it would be advisable to have two judges of the superior court and a judge of the local district adjudicate on these appeals. It is not at all that we have not faith or confidence in those who are hearing these appeals at the present time. It is simply a question of putting too much power into the hands of one man. If you have three judges hearing the appeals you will get a fair judgment; perhaps what one of the three overlooks the other two will not, and there will be argument in that connection. I have the greatest admiration for the Minister of Justice, but the feeling of the people is that we are putting too great a power into the hands of one man. I know that we can depend on the minister to do the job well and fairly, but so long as it is done by one man there is suspicion and unrest among the people with respect to any decision he may make. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I urge that the appeals should be decided by a body of three judges, and *where they disagree the minister could make the final decision. I

mention this simply because I feel that we must get away from the suspicion that there is in connection with the internment of some of these people.
The committee which considered the defence of Canada regulations last year did a wonderful job. Naturally we all hate to see our privileges taken away from us-habeas corpus, the right of free speech, and all those things. But wre all recognize the necessity for some curtailment of our liberties in time of war. I believe that if action is taken along the lines I have indicated, the people of this country, especially the new Canadians, will be much better satisfied and have far more confidence in the administration of the defence of Canada regulations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate the house on the tone of this debate, and I am grateful to hon. members for many of the things that have been said. There is no doubt that the committee which will sit on the defence of Canada regulations will keep in mind 'the suggestions that have been made in the course of the debate. The most critical speeches have been one by the hon. member for North Battleford (Mrs. Nielsen) and, to some extent, one by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas). I am sorry that my hon. friend the member for North Battleford is not at present in the chamber because I have to refer to her remarks and also to something that she said outside the house in recent months.
First, I should like to clear up a matter which was discussed last year and again in the course of this debate with regard to the alleged confiscation of copies of speeches of the hon. member for North Battleford in Saskatchewan and elsewhere. I regret that when this question was raised a few months ago, I was absent by reason of an indisposition that lasted for some time, and I could not give the explanations which I desire to make to-day.

Defence of Canada-Special Committee
In the first place, it was not the speech delivered by the hon. member for North Babtleford that was seized, but a leaflet, a copy of which I have in my hand, entitled "Why I Opposed the Budget". It is substantially a reiteration of the hon. member's speech with a few changes which later, when that speech was inserted with others in a pamphlet published by the Canadian Tribune, were eliminated. For instance, the words:
You have been told by press and radio that this budget was patriotic, that it ensured equality of sacrifice and equal participation in the war effort. That is a lie, and. this war budget is instead the greatest hoax ever perpetrated on the nation.
"That is a lie" was not said in the House of Commons, and I congratulate the hon. member that it was eliminated from the copy of her speech which is now in a pamphlet which I have here with other speeches printed and published and distributed by the Canadian Tribune.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND REVIEW REGULATIONS AND NATURALIZATION AND DEPORTATION LAW'S
speechtext: Was there anything subversive about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND REVIEW REGULATIONS AND NATURALIZATION AND DEPORTATION LAW'S
speechtext:
That is a question of opinion. It was considered such. The question did not come to us at the time. As my hon. friend knows, in Saskatchewan, as in many other provinces, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police act under the direction of the attorney general of the province. These were not pamphlets, I may say, because the last pamphlets have never been confiscated. These were leaflets. They were taken over by the police and were studied by the law officers of the government of Saskatchewan. They considered that perhaps it was better not to proceed, and the leaflets were returned to those from whom they had been taken. That is the whole situation.
In the city of Edmonton there is a gentleman-I do not know whether I should give the name-who has been under observation for a long time. He is the distributor of communist literature in that city and has been selling copies of the Moscow News, published in Moscow, a publication which has been prohibited in Canada since August last. During the latter part of August that man was seen with a certain quantity of leaflets and a search warrant was issued by the authorities in Regina. Four hundred copies of the leaflet "Why I Opposed the Budget" were found in his place. They were referred to the attorney general's department for decision. No action was taken and the leaflets were subsequently returned to the man.
The same thing happened in Regina, too. On my memorandum here there are two other names of people who have been handling
communist literature. The leaflets were found and were surrendered by these men and they did not; wish to take them back, so they were not given back to them. They did not want them.
The same thing happened with regard to an organization called the Regina Workers' Protective Organization. There also they handed the leaflets to the police and did not wish to have them back. It was found that these leaflets had been printed by Eveready Printing and Publishing Company of Toronto. At the premises of the Canadian Tribune Publishing Company, a few proofs and five copies of the pamphlet were seized, but following examination and reference to the Attorney General of Saskatchewan, they were returned to Mr. Macleod on November 25.
A summary of all this-and I think the house will realize that too much noise has been made under the circumstances-is this:
(1)	The investigation centred around the leaflet "Why I Opposed the Budget," not around the speeches in the House of Commons or the pamphlets which were subsequently published.
(2)	The leaflet was not a speech made in the House of Commons. (3) No individuals were arrested. (4) No persons were intimidated. (5) The leaflet and pamphlet were not suppressed. As a matter of fact, the pamphlet has already had its third printing since then, the second and third issues omitting the open letter to Canadians. (6) The investigation differed in no way from any other similar inquiry.
I must say to my hon. friend the member for North Battleford that really she has not been treated as terribly as she would like us to believe. She certainly has not been hampered in her activities. As an hon. member has just stated, she has gone throughout the country making speeches, and I must say that her language this afternoon was very mild compared with what she has been stating on the platforms. It is true she has said that the defence of Canada regulations should be called the defence of capital regulations. But that is far less than what the hon. member has been saying all over the country. I have here reports of her speeches throughout the land; they are about the same everywhere.

I may say that the hon. member did not do justice to herself in her speech this afternoon when she denounced fascism in the most violent vray but said never a word about communism. Let me quote further:
The defence of Canada regulations have caused fear to be instilled in the hearts of the people. Look back a number of years and remember how so many immigrants came to this country seeking freedom of religion, but now such is not the case. Jehovah's Witnesses are now an illegal organization, they cannot now gather together to worship as they please.
If we are going to call ourselves democrats we should not deny ourselves the privileges we want to enjoy. The same thing happened in Germany. Take for instance Pastor Niemoller.
As the war goes on not only our privileges are cut down by the defence of Canada regulations but monopoly has taken steps through the medium of prices, wages, et cetera.
The trade union movement was trying to prevent these things but they are now being prevented.
She then quoted from a letter supposed to have been received from a member of the United Electrical and Radio Workers in Toronto which quoted an article giving details of labour conditions in Germany in 1940, and the writer compares them with conditions in Canada. At Winnipeg she quoted from an article in a Toronto paper which outlined the long hours and hardships which the German people had to endure, and she said that these very things, "which we are fighting against", existed in Canada.
Of course, as far as the government is concerned, in her view it is very bad. She repeated everywhere that we are a few Charlie McCarthys sitting on the lap of big business; "no more democracy in Canada"; "democracy destroyed"-and she said that this afternoon. Is the hon. lady member fair to her country of adoption? I believe she has been treated pretty fairly by Canada,

Mr. LAPOINTE (Quebec East). Is this fair? The mere fact that a lady member can make the speech she made this afternoon, and can speak as she did throughout the country during a war as is the situation at present, shows that we still have democracy. Does the hon. lady member believe that she

must have limits. She says that these defence of Canada restrictions may continue after the war. She did pay me the compliment of saying that she thought I was sincere, and as Minister of Justice would see that they are removed, but she is afraid that some other minister of justice may come. In this she is not like some newspapers who seem to hope that some other will come. But she forgets this: the defence of Canada regulations are enacted under the authority of the War Measures Act, the last clause of which provides that the act ends with the last day of the war. Therefore my hon. friend need not have any misgivings about that. All these restrictions are essentially temporary, for a time of emergency, and end with the emergency.
I should not like to say anything that might offend the hon. member in any way. If, however, the police have searched for those leaflets, of which search she complained so strongly, it is because my hon. friend keeps bad company, very bad company indeed.

friend if she wants to see it. I am sure, however, my hon. friend would repudiate any association with those people and would rather associate with other members of the house in order to give help to those carrying on the war effort of Canada, to help us all achieve victory and peace.
May I make one other observation. This morning I was reading the report of a lecture given yesterday in Montreal by a European woman who stated that in Germany and other fascist countries women are barred from all public activities and have no rights except that of raising families. When my hon. friend says we have destroyed democracy in Canada, I do not think she is being altogether fair to Canada. Here ladies like my hon. friend can exercise all their rights; they are free in all their activities, and certainly my hon. friend is using that right to the limit of her capacity.
I have nothing more to add, except that in fairness to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police I thought I ought to give the facts with regard to this matter. The police have also asked me to answer a certain statement made in the Toronto Saturday Night of March 1 in an article by Politicus, headed "Mr. Lapointe, What do you Say?" Of course, I cannot say anything, because I did not read it. This is an extract from that article:
Politicus knows of two cases of newspaper people of the highest loyalty and integrity whom the R.C.M.P. are investigating and on whom they have a dossier. And in neither of those eases, both journalists being people whom Politicus knows well, is there the slightest doubt of their anxiety, perhaps over anxiety, if there can be such a thing, for Britain to win this wrar, and of their responsibility.
The commissioner tells me that he has made inquiries and is able to say that he knows of no one, male or female, connected with newspapers, whom this force is investigating or has investigated since the outbreak of war, with the possible exception of Harry Binder, who is now serving a sentence. Why should these statements be made, creating disaffection and nervousness among the public? Some days ago a letter, written by a Toronto lawyer who represents communists who are interned, was drawn to my attention. In that letter he attacked me personally, saying that of course I could not do justice to trade unionists because I am from Quebec and in Quebec people are against labour syndicates. In this statement there are two falsehoods.
First, Quebec is not against labour unions; far from it. Quebec was the pioneer in labour legislation. Second, as far as I am concerned, if that man knows me he knows I have been fighting for the trade unions all my life. I have been fighting against those employers who have been reluctant to permit the establishment of trade unions in their factories. I have been fighting for the right of labour to bargain collectively. So why say these things? Of course I am not surprised. I have a difficult task; I am doing it to the best of my capacity. I have been told in persuasive fashion that I should do things in a certain way; I have also received threats, and I may say that I have been advised indirectly that if a certain gentleman were not released I might expect a newspaper campaign. Neither sweet inducements nor threats will have any influence on me. I will do what I think is right whatever may be the consequences; and if the committee changes the regulations and I still have something to do with them, I will apply them as I think they should be applied. Again, neither inducement, blackmail nor threats will have any influence.

Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING
(Prime Minister) moved:
That a select committee be appointed to examine the expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, and for other services directly connected with the war, and to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein, and that notwithstanding standing order 65 the committee shall consist of twenty-four members, as follows:	Messrs. Abbott,
Bercovitch, Black (Cumberland), Bradette, Chevrier, Cleaver, Diefenbaker, Fournier (Hull), Gladstone, Golding. Graham, Gray, Green, Harris (Danforth), Macdonald (Halifax). Maclnnis, Marshall, Mayhew, MeGeer, Picard, Bottler, Ross (Moose Jaw), Sissons, Thorson, with power to send for persons, papers and records; to examine witnesses and to report from time to time to the house.
He said: At the outset may I explain the significance of the reference in the motion to the expression "notwithstanding standing order 65". No doubt hon. members are familiar with that standing order, but I might say in a word it is to the effect that no special committee may, without leave of the house, consist of more than fifteen persons. Hon. members will notice that provision is made in this resolution for a committee of twenty-four persons.
It may help to place the motion in its true light were I to review the circumstances which have led me to present it to the house in the form in which it appears upon the order paper. At this stage of the session, after a long adjournment, we are apt to forget that the session itself began on November 7, continued until December 6, and that we reconvened on February 17. I mention this because before the adjournment had taken place there had been an agreement on. the part of the government to introduce the motion which is now before us-at least, this motion, with a slight alteration.
Hon. members will recall that shortly after the session began, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) suggested that the house should consider the appointment of two select committees, one which, from a factual and objective point of view, would have to report upon the fighting forces, army, navy and air, and another which would be concerned with questions of supplies and deliveries of equipment, munitions and the like.
At the time he suggested consideration of the appointment of two such committees, my

War Expenditures-Special Committee
hon. friend said that he recognized the implications, and that he thought perhaps it would be preferable, before any steps were taken, to have a conference between himself and some members of his party and myself, as leader of the government, and some members of the government.
That conference took place, and it was, I believe, in part as a result of it that, when my hon. friend the leader of the opposition returned to the subject in this house, he brought forward what he termed a concrete suggestion, one which he said he believed was constructive. It was an invitation to the government to consider the appointment of a committee for the control of national expenditures, which would be on all fours with the similar committee in the United Kingdom. My hon. friend read to the house the order which set forth the powers and terms of reference of the committee in the United Kinggdom, and stated that he had in his possession copies of the reports of that committee, that he believed its work had been very useful, and that, for these reasons, he would recommend to the government the appointment of such a committee.
Very shortly after he made that announcement, or proposal, I told my hon. friend that the government would accept it, and that we would be prepared to appoint a committee along the lines of the committee in the United Kingdom with respect to the control of national expenditures. Within a day or two before the house adjourned I gave the definite assurance to the house that, as soon as parliament reassembled, I would introduce the motion, and that the committee would be appointed.
Since the recess, I believe on the first day of the reassembling of parliament, the leader of the opposition asked me, as the record will show, what decision had been reached with respect to the setting up of the committee on the control of national expenditures. I said to my hon. friend in reply that I was prepared to bring in the motion at once. The only reason I was not doing so at that time was that the motion required notice, and that, before introducing the motion, I wished to get from the whips the names of the members who would compose the committee. The leader of the opposition then suggested it would be well if we should have a further conference before the motion was introduced. He thought that the terms of reference were as important as the membership of the committee, and said that he would like to have a further conference with me. I agreed to that immediately and my hon. friend did -have a further conference, at which time I thought
we had reached complete agreement as to the terms of reference, and I so reported to my colleagues in the cabinet.
Subsequently, however, my hon. friend met me in company with one of the members of his party and suggested consideration of a change in the wording of the resolution. At that time I gave him my reasons for feeling that the resolution should not be changed. It was agreed, however, to have a further conference between my hon. friend and one or two members of his party and myself along with one or two of my colleagues, and that further conference was held. To-day I bring in the motion as it has been modified as a result of the first conference I held with my hon. friend immediately after parliament reassembled.
It is most important that the circumstances which have led up to the appointment of this committee should be carefully reviewed and understood because I regret to say that within the last few days there has been a great deal of misrepresentation concerning the purpose of the government in proposing this committee. The fact has been completely forgotten that the proposal was made by the leader of the opposition himself and that it was accepted in full by the government. As I have said, we -had reached agreement on the matter before parliament adjourned in December last. An entirely different construction has been placed upon the motion from that which was intended, I believe, by my hon. friend at the outset or by myself in accepting it. The government's whole position in the matter has been so completely misrepresented and misconstrued-

I am coming
to that-by what has appeared in a section of the press within the last few days-I am not saying that my hon. friend has misconstrued it-that I think it is most important that the whole matter should be caTefu-lly reviewed. I would remind hon. members that when parliament is in session, political battles may be fought in two places, either in parliament or throughout the country. When we are being told that the opposition in the House of Commons is anxious to cooperate with the government and to do all that it possibly can so to do, we rather expect that the opposition press throughout the country will adopt a similar attitude or at least that it will withhold criticism of a measure, and above all misinterpretation of a measure, until it has been fully discussed on the floor of the house.
