War Expenditures-Special Committee
Because I recognize that this is a very important measure I purpose going rather carefully into the different steps which have led to the motion being presented to-day in the form in which it is by the government. First, I would refer to what my hon. friend the leader of the opposition said with regard to the appointment of committees of this house which might serve the purpose of giving the public more information on the manner in which our war effort is being carried on, and more in the way of control of expenditures in connection with the war effort. Page 43 of Hansard of November 12, 1940, sets forth the first reference which my hon. friend made to the advisability of establishing select committees of the house to deal with war effort matters. My hon. friend is reported as having said:
.... I am impelled to propose to the government that it cause to be set up immediately two select special committees which will be charged with the responsibility and the duty of investigating and reporting to this house factually, objectively and truthfully, without bias and without partisanship-and I have no doubt that is possible-what is our exact position (a) with respect to our fighting forces, military, naval and air; and (b) with respect to the production and delivery of all the important materials, equipment and supplies necessary in our war effort, so that the Canadian people may know the truth. Before such committees ministers could appear and be subject to questioning.
A little further on, my hon. friend said:
The government may hold the view that it is not in the public interest that the facts and figures for which I am asking be disclosed. I know the matter is not free from difficulties. When I make the proposal I visualize many of its implications,

And a little further on:
I am willing with some of my colleagues to meet with the Prime Minister and some of his colleagues so that we may consider the whole proposal, in an honest effort to arrive at a conclusion.
That was the first suggestion made in this house for the appointment of special committees to deal with the war effort. May I say a word as to the manner in which that suggestion was received? A conference between my hon. friend and some of his colleagues and myself and some of my colleagues took place shortly after. The subject came up again in the house on December 3. At that time the leader of the opposition made reference to the former occasion on which he had suggested the appointment of these two committees. At pages 615 and

616 of Hansard of December 3, 1940, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition is reported as follow's:
So far, such committees have not been set up. I indicated that I knew there were difficulties, and I would ask the Prime Minister, if he can and will, to tell the house what the attitude of the government is with respect to that. If the difficulties are such as cannot be surmounted then I have another concrete suggestion which I desire to lay before the house and the country. It is, in brief, that the government cause to be set up a select committee on current expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, for civil defence and for other services directly connected with the war, and instruct such committee to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of government policies may be effected therein.
Now, it is all very well to say that we can get all this information on national expenditure through the public accounts committee. Theoretically that is correct. But the information which will be obtained through the public accounts idea will not be on current expenditure. It w'ill relate only to the expenditures that have taken place in the previous year and as covered by the auditor general's report. Practically all the national expenditure for the war effort has taken place since March 31 last-or rather the great bulk of the contracts relating to national expenditure for war effort have been let since March 31, and inquiry before the public accounts committee will not be possible. That committee may examine only such things as are submitted to it. I am impelled to make this request for various reasons, but more particularly because what I suggest has been done in England and, I am advised, with good results.
I hold in my hand a series of reports of a select standing committee of the British parliament which was set up under the authority of an order of reference made on December 12, 1939, while Mr. Chamberlain was still Prime Minister and while there was an official opposition. The order of reference contains this:
My hon. friend then goes on to quote from the order of reference. If hon. members will keep in mind the wording of the motion which is before the house at the present time, they will see that the two references are identical except for a word or two. My hon. friend goes on to quote the order of reference as follows:
That a select committee be appointed to examine the current expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, for civil defence and for other services directly connected with the war, and to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein.
Continuing with the words of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition:
Then it goes on and appoints a committee of twenty-eight members-and not one of them is a member of the government; they are all private members, and so far as I read the list of names, none of them are of international prominence. The committee has the usual power to send for persons, papers and records,

War Expenditures-Special Committee
and to sit notwithstanding any adjournment of the house, and to adjourn from place to place. It was to be in effect a continuous working committee to examine current expenditures for war purposes having regard to the announced policy of the government. It had the power to appoint subcommittees and to refer to such subcommittees any of the matters within the jurisdiction of the committee. Such subcommittees so appointed were empowered to send for persons, papers and records, to sit notwithstanding any adjournment of the house, and to adjourn from place to place. This select committee has been sitting almost constantly since it was set up. Its first report was made in January, and the last I have was made on August 21, 1940. Any hon. gentleman who peruses this report will see, I am sure, that it is serving a great national purpose-not in opposition to government policy, not to the detriment of government policy, but to assist government policy, and to see what if any economies can be attained by suggestions.
My view is that we ought to have something like that here in Canada. It is a way in which private members could contribute to the war effort. I have heard dozens of members who support the government bewail the fact that they could not do anything to help, and saying that private members ought to be in a position to do something to help.
Then my hon. friend, a little further on,
says:
I submit this to the government as a constructive proposal to which they should give some attention. I submit it in the utmost good faith, not by way of criticism but by way of being helpful to the government. We know that war is wasteful; we know there is great waste in this war, though I do not say intentional waste. I do believe, however, that a committee of private members of this house, sitting day in and day out during sessions and between sessions, could perform a very useful function in assisting the government at this time, and I commend this suggestion to hon. members. It will provide an outlet for the energies of the private members who are anxious about the war, who want to make a contribution, who were sent here by their constituents to make that contribution but who find themselves frustrated-yes, that is the word-because they have no outlet for their abilities and their capabilities.
My hon. friend goes on:
I do hope that the Prime Minister will acept this suggestion, and before I leave the topic may I say to hon. gentlemen who will accept positions on the committee, if it be set up: There is not only a real job to he done, but a job which will tax your capabilities to the utmost. You will have to make substantial sacrifices in serving the state in this way, but it is a patriotic duty which I think some of you ought to perform. I believe a real contribution can be made in this way by private members.
May I pause again to remind the house that the motion before it which I have presented to-day is an acceptance in full, and going somewhat further, as I shall indicate a few moments later, of the proposal of the hon. leader of the opposition, made, I assume,
after consultation with members of his party and with his party solidly behind him in making that proposal.
What were the grounds on which the leader of the opposition put forward the proposal for this committee on the control of national expenditures? First of all, he advanced it as a concrete suggestion, as a constructive suggestion. He commended it and presented it to the government and asked its acceptance more particularly on two grounds: on what had been done in England, and done there with good results, and as serving a great national purpose, namely, to assist government policy, to effect economies and to avoid waste. There was the further purpose, to enable private members to contribute to the war effort, to afford an outlet to the energies of private members to perform a patriotic duty. Let me draw attention to the wording of the resolution which the leader of the opposition proposed. The first point in it is that the government cause to be set up a select committee on current expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, for civil defence and for other services directly connected with the war.
It was a request for a committee to deal with current expenditures. Second, such committee was to be instructed to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of government policies may be effected therein.
The motion as presented by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition or which he was asking me to present was that the committee should report with respect to economies, to avoid waste and the like, and to report with respect to economies which would be consistent with the execution of government policies. It was not for any other purpose.
I do not think there can be any doubt, Mr. Speaker, about the leader of the opposition having made the proposal, or about the exact nature of it, the scope of it, the purpose of it, and of his having strengthened his position by saying it was precisely the same motion that had carried in the United Kingdom, under which a committee in the United Kingdom was operating to-day.
What attitude did I take towards the suggestion? My reply to my hon. friend will be found in Hansard of December 3 at page 633. Speaking in reply to the leader of the opposition, I said:
A few days ago my hon. friend spoke of the desirability of the house appointing two standing committees. I believe he made that suggestion on November 12. when he first spoke in this debate. His words were as follows.
1222	COMMONS
War Expenditures-Special Committee
Then I quoted the words which I have already given the house to revive its memory. I mentioned also my hon. friend having suggested that there should be a conference between himself and his colleagues and myself and certain of my colleagues. Then I continued as follows:
May I say that since making that statement, my hon. friend and two of his colleagues have met with me and two or three of my colleagues to consider the matter there referred to. I wish to say to him and to the house-
I ask hon. members to note the manner in which I as leader of the government sought to accept the suggestion made by the leader of the opposition:
I wish to say to him and to the house that no approach to the subject could have been more helpful or could have been better in every respect than that which he and his colleagues made in confidence with the government in this matter. We spoke quite frankly to my hon. friend and his colleagues with respect to the difficulties which surrounded the procedure of dealing with war expenditures, questions of production and distribution-deliveries, I believe, was the word he used-in any standing committee of the house which might be holding its proceedings in public and which during part of the time might have to ask that the proceedings be held for some time in camera. We particularly pointed out the difficulties of imparting to parliament or to any committees certain information.
I will mention to the house just what one of those difficulties is. We have been asked by the British government-and this is a request they have made to governments in all parts of the British commonwealth; it is not one which has been made to us alone; it is a matter of which the British government itself has taken full account-to avoid, if possible, the disclosure of numbers, the disclosure of amounts, the disclosure of quantities, the disclosure of anything in public which would help to give the enemy an appreciation of the strength or lack of strength of the forces opposing him.
I think every one can see the reasonableness of a position of the kind. But it does raise a very difficult situation for the government. If we are not on the horns of a dilemma, we are at least in the matter of information sailing between Scylla and Charybdis all the time. We are either too near the rock of Scylla in giving more in the way of information than we should, or we are drifting to the other side toward the whirlpool of Charybdis and are being accused of withholding from the people of our country the information they are entitled to have.
I oan only put the situation as it is in its clear light before members of this house and before the country, and trust to the soundness of their judgment. That is the position we are in with respect to the disclosure of information that might prove to be harmful.
A little further on, I said:
It is for that reason and for that reason only that the government hesitates to say to this house that it is prepared to have standing committees before which will be placed the exact position with respect to our fighting forces, naval, military and air.
	*
And further:
I agree with what my hon. friend has said about the position of private members in this house. Every member is -anxious -to become more actively interested in Canada's war effort.
And further on:
Hon. members are right in feeling that they would wish, that the house itself would wish to make its own contribution to the war effort in some way.
And later on:
I can assure hon. members that we desire their fullest cooperation.
Having given, as my hon. friend had asked me to do, the reasons why we felt that it would not be wise to accept the suggestion of the two committees he had spoken of, I then gave my acceptance of the proposal which he made, and I did so in the following words:
This afternoon my hon. friend made a suggestion which appeals very strongly to me for more reasons -than one; first of all, because of the proposal itself, and also because it is the procedure which on -this very perplexing matter h-as been adopted at Westminster. In the parliament at Westminster the government has been faced with exactly the same situation we are faced with here. They have of course a much larger number of private members than we have in -this House of Commons and their private members are as anxious to make their contribution as are our private members.
Then further on:
The British government are making expenditures on a much vaster scale than we are, and human nature -is the same in -the United Kingdom as it is -in Canada with reg-ard -to all classes and conditions of men and how they may -act in respect of government contracts and large quantities of money and supplies at a time of war. They are just as anxious -as we -are to see -that whatever is done is done openly, honestly and -above-board and to bring to time summarily -anyone who seeks to profit by opportunities which war conditions may afford. But they have not thought it advisable to set up standing committees of the character which was originally proposed by the leader of the opposition. They h-ave, however, established a committee on national expenditure which has been given certain powers and which has been functioning now for almost a year, having been set up on December 12, 1939.
I then read the motion, which I have already repeated several times, setting forth the powers which are given to the committee on national expenditure in Great Britain; and having quoted the resolution which had been proposed by my hon. friend, I said:
.... may I say that after careful consideration of the whole matter the government is prepared to introduce -a similar motion into this house and to follow -the procedure which has been adopted by Westminster with respect to war expenditure.

TEnr Expenditures-Special Committee
That was a full acceptance of my hon. friend's proposal-full with respect to all the terms of reference, going, indeed, a step further by declaring that we were prepared to follow, with regard to the procedure of the committee itself, the example which had been set at Westminster. That acceptance was given without reservation, mental or otherwise. It was given in a whole-hearted, open and frank manner, deeply appreciative of what, at that time at all events, I believed was the desire on the part of the opposition to cooperate with the government in this matter and which I believe to be still the desire that actuates my hon. friend the leader of the opposition.
I come now to a very important point, namely, what in the mind of the leader of the opposition and my mind as leader of the government, and having the responsibility I have in this time of war, was to be the exact character of this committee, whether it was to be a committee, as its terms set forth, to help to control national expenditure, to give to private members of the house their opportunity to make a contribution towards Canada's war effort in the manner therein indicated, or whether it was to be an instrument of party political warfare, that this house was to give to some committee a general warrant to search for scandal.

Yes, a fishing expedition, a x-oving committee. I thought it was important to make the purpose clear in the interests of both the opposition and the government; also that it should be perfectly understood by the country in this time of war what the motive was that lay behind the proposal and what was to be its purpose when the committee was formed. In doing so I used the following words:
I want to add that whoever is appointed to such a committee ought to take his responsibilities very seriously. Great care will have to he taken in the selection of the personnel. If there is a genuine desire to do the thing that is helpful, I am sure that great good can come out of the existence of a committee of the kind. If, on the other hand, the committee is to be made an instrument for party warfare, I cannot conceive of anything that could be worse.
That is on page 635 of Hansard.
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury): May I interrupt my right hon. friend to say that nothing was further from my thoughts.
Mr. Mackenzie King: Quite so. I have not said that my hon. friend-
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury): I am not looking for scandal.
Mr. Mackenzie King: I believe that my hon friend is wholly sincere in what he says. I would not have made the remark I did had I thought that he was not. But I repeat that if a committee of the kind were to be used as an instrument of party political warfare, I cannot conceive of a way of working greater injury to Canada's war effort. But a committee which takes its responsibilities seriously, and will assist the government in exercising a control over the expenditures which are being made, keeping on the government the responsibility for policy, but being free to make suggestions that will be helpful and constructive, should be of the greatest possible service. It was that kind of committee which on December 12 last was set up at Westminster, and this is the motion under which action was taken.
I then read the motion, and I went on:
I propose, Mr. Speaker, as soon as parliament reassembles after the adjournment, to introduce a motion in those words in this House of Commons.
I said that the reason for waiting until after parliament reassembled was that I thought it would be a better time to select the members of the committee, and I concluded with these words:
I hope this assurance will meet with general acceptance.
May I conclude before recess by quoting one article which represents, I believe, the impression that was left at the end of the session as to the satisfactory nature of the proceedings between the opposition and the government. The opposition were getting a good deal of credit for having put forward a constructive proposal; the government on its part was being commended for having accepted1 the proposal, and the country generally seemed quite satisfied with the action which was to be taken. I shall read but this one article. It is from the Toronto Globe and Mail of December 5, 1940, being an editorial headed "Will Ensure Confidence":
The Prime Minister's acquiescence in the suggestion of Mr. Hanson for a parliamentary committee to inquire into war expenditures will be approved in the country as it was in the Commons. The select committee to be set up when parliament reassembles on February 17 will be composed of representatives of all parties in proportion to their strength in the house. If the committee follows the precedent of Westminster it will hold some of its sittings in camera. The quality of its membership should be high if the inquiry is to ascertain whether the country is getting full value for the whole of its expenditure.
Sheer fault-finding is not an indulgence for which there can be any patience or excuse when the nation is fighting for its life. Any attempt to make political capital which would retard the war effort will be severely condemned. What the public wants to know is whether economies can be effected without slowing up preparations for the defeat of Hitlerism. The committee should have ample power to examine expendi-
1224	COMMONS
War Expenditures-Special Committee
tures for the defence services and for other services directly connected with the war. If it can suggest economies which will in no way hamper the war effort it will do well.
There may be a disposition to exploit the opportunity to discredit the government, but Mr. Hanson was prompt in giving assurance that there was no such thought in his mind. The supreme concern should be to accomplish something that will promote efficiency and economy without impairing the nation's striking force.
The government's decision to create a parliamentary committee to examine expenditures and to suggest what, if any, economies can be made will in itself inspire public confidence.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, when, the house recessed, I had concluded discussing the resolution now before us as respects what had taken place during the period of the session before adjournment. I pointed out that the resolution at present before the house is almost identical with the one which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) suggested should be adopted by the government; I indicated the steps which had led the government to accept the resolution in substantially the wording presented by the leader of the opposition, and stated that when parliament adjourned I had thought both sides of the house were in complete agreement as to the resolution and its terms of reference. What I believe justifies that view is the fact that, as I have indicated, the press of the country generally seemed to entertain it. I think it was a logical view to take having regard to the emphasis which my hon. friend the leader of the opposition placed on the practice at Westminster and the emphasis which I personally am inclined to place upon that practice as an example in matters of procedure here.
I wish now to say a word or two about what has happened since parliament reassembled. The leader of the opposition referred to the matter of this committee on Monday, February 17, the first day the house met, and his remarks will be found at page 789 of Hansard. Speaking on the business of the house, the leader of the opposition said:
May I also ask the Prime Minister if he will be good enough to let us know when the proposed committee on national expenditure will be set up.
I ask the house to note those words, "will be set up." I think the question of my hon. friend makes quite clear by itself that in his mind at that time there was agreement on the committee and that the committee would be

set up. I omitted to reply to that question at the time, and at. page 863 of Hansard my hon. friend is reported as follows:
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury): There was the question of the setting up of a committee on national expenditure.
Mr. Mackenzie King: I am sorry I omitted to refer to that. 1 hope to introduce the motion this week. I would have introduced it at once, but I thought it desirable that the whips should first confer as to the personnel of the committee. It is also necessary under the rules of the house that notice shall be given in the Votes and Proceedings . . .
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury): May I interject that I think it would be very desirable that we should confer on the terms of reference to the committee. That I think is just as important as the personnel of the committee.
Mr. Mackenzie King: I shall be very happy to confer with my hon. friend. I may say I had in mind in drafting the motion what he himself had expressed before the adjournment, namely, that we should follow as closely as possible the motion as introduced in the British House of Commons. I have had the motion prepared, but I shall be pleased to confer with my hon. friend further with regard to it.
The leader of the opposition, made one other reference to the matter on February 19, appearing at page 835 of Hansard, when for the first time there was a new feature introduced. This is what he said:
I hope that the committee on national expenditure, when set up, will examine and criticize all expenditures for war purposes, past, present and future, and award praise or blame, as the case may be.
You will observe, Mr. Speaker, that my hon. friend's motion had dealt with current expenditures; but now for the first time this new feature was introduced.
. . . will examine and criticize all expenditures for war purposes, past, present and future, and award praise or blame, as the case may be. But the government must not evade or seek to evade responsibility because of the existence of this committee, and the powers of the committee must not be limited to reporting on methods of controlling expenditure. The committee must have power to report on expenditures already made, and the responsibility of refusing to go that far in the order of reference will be upon the government, and upon the government alone.
Apparently this widening of the terms of the resolution was an afterthought, the result evidently of discussion between my hon. friend and some of his followers.
In accordance with the promise I gave my hon. friend at the time, I met him in conference. With him was his colleague the hon. member for Y7ale (Mr. Stirling), and I had with me my colleague the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), who is with me at the present time. If I am not mistaken, this was on February 19. We discussed the resolution, and during that discussion I had in my hand the document which I have before me

War Expenditures-Special Committee
at the present time. These conferences are supposed to be confidential. I am prepared., to have them so regarded, if that is desired; or I am quite prepared to have everything that was said at the conferences made public here, if that is thought to be preferable. But I would point out to the house that I am in an embarrassing position, in this respect; that while confidence apparently is being kept between the leader of the opposition and myself with regard to what has taken place at certain conferences, the press of the country has been told of all sorts of happenings and discussions. They have begun to base their editorials on this hearsay and have found reason to take exception to the government's alleged action.

speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for drawing attention to the fact that the reports that have appeared certainly were perverted, I would say, and utterly lacking in justification.
I hope my hon. friend will not object to my referring to the terms of reference of the resolution as discussed in conference with him and the hon. member for Yale, because that will enable me to clear up one matter which I think is most important, inasmuch as it is one which has given rise to most of the discussion outside. I refer to the term of reference which was agreed to at the first conference between my hon. friend the leader of the opposition and myself, and which the cabinet subsequently approved. The resolution proposed by my hon. friend to be presented to the house read as follows:
That a select committee be appointed to examine the current expenditures defrayed out of the moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, for civil defence and for other services directly connected with the war, and to report what, if any. economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein.
My attention was drawn in the conference to the use of the word "current" which appears in the resolution. It appears in the order under which the British parliament is proceeding. The leader of the opposition said he thought the word "current" might be misunderstood, that it might give rise to the impression that the government was trying
to draw a hard and fast line, that it wished only to examine into current expenditures, and that other expenditures would be found in the auditor general's report, which would be referred to the committee on public accounts. He thought the word "current" ought to be eliminated.
I wish to make perfectly clear, first of all, that the British government have maintained a hard and fast line between current expenditures, which are being inquired into by the committee at Westminster, and past expenditures which, it takes the position, can be looked into only by the public accounts committee.
I agreed with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition that leaving the word "current" in might lead to some misunderstanding, or might create some suspicion, and I said that I wTould be agreeable to striking it out; that so far as I was concerned I was quite prepared to have the committee clothed with power to inquire into all expenditures which related to the war, going back to the commencement of the war, if they so desired and believed it to be in the public interest so to do. I made that very clear, and agreed with him then and there, without conference with my colleagues, to strike out the word "current." But I said I would wish to get approval of the cabinet before giving any final word in the matter to the house.
There were one or two other words we also thought might as well go out. I refer to the words "for civil defence" in the clause "provided by parliament for the defence services, for civil defence and for other services." The words "for civil defence" which appear in the British resolution we did not think were necessary in the resolution to be put before this parliament. In the British resolution I believe the term "civil defence" has reference particularly to A.R.P. personnel and to the registration they have in England of persons offering technical and professional services in connection with the war effort. At any rate the words "for the defence sendees and for services directly connected with the war" we felt would cover all that could be included in "for civil defence."
Therefore it was agreed at that conference on February 19 that the resolution would read:
. . . committee be appointed to examine the expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, and for other services directly connected with the war, and to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein.
I shall come in a few minutes to what has taken place by way of criticism of the government by a section of the press of our country,

1226	COMMONS
War Expenditures-Special Committee
in advance of the presentation to-day of the resolution I have in nay hand. But before taking up that aspect of the matter, I wish to point out why the government feels the resolution we are now presenting, in the broad terms to Which I have just referred, should be accepted-and accepted 'as it is, without subtraction and without addition.
In a word it is this: We believe at this time of war it is advisable to follow the practice at Westminster with respect to all matters of procedure affecting the war, unless we have the best of good reasons for departing therefrom. If there is any reason why we should adopt in this parliament with regard to this matter a resolution different from that which has been adopted at Westminster, and if such reason is a material one, I shall be the first to be prepared to consider the re-wording of the resolution now before us. But I would not take upon myself the responsibility in this parliament, knowing of the zeal and care taken by the British parliament in connection with all matters respecting its public expenditures, of taking any step in some unforeseen direction at this time. It is for that reason that my colleagues and I feel that, having before us a resolution on Which the British parliament is acting to-day, we are justified in presenting that resolution to this house, and that we would not be justified in making a material change in its terms.
But there is a further reason, and it is this: The resolution in the British House of Commons governing waT expenditures is not one which has been presented to the British House of Commons for the first time either this year or last year. To all intents and purposes this resolution follows one which was passed in the British parliament in 1917, at the time of the last war. I would point out that on that occasion the war had run on for three years before in the British parliament any committee was appointed to deal with war expenditures. I might at this point refer to the action-or lack of action-in this parliament at that time. There was no committee appointed during the last war such as is being granted by this government under the resolution now before the house. No such committee was granted during the whole of the war period. But in Great Britain in 1917, after three years of war, the government did agree to the appointment of a committee along the lines set forth herein.
At that time every argument which could be put forward either for or against the resolution was, I believe, presented in the British House of Commons. The matter was fully discussed. The question of whether

expenditures should be current expenditures or all expenditures, the question of whether the terms of the resolution should be broadened in any particular, the question of whether there should be a restriction as to matter's relating to economy, and restrictions with respect to action being in accord with the policy of the government-all of these matters were carefully examined and discussed, by question and answer, by the opposition and the ministry, and at the end of it all the committee was appointed, without any division.
I have in my hand some of the statements made at that time. I believe they throw light upon the work the committee was intended to perform, and the reasons why the terms of reference are drafted as they are. At that time Mr. Herbert Samuel, now Lord Samuel, was leader of the opposition. Mr. Lloyd George was leader of the government, and Mr. Bonar Law was leader of the House of Commons, and spoke for the government in the house. The British Hansard for July 6, 1917, reports Mr. Samuel's observations. In the same issue will be found the words of the other gentlemen whom I have mentioned.
Mr. Samuel1, speaking as leader of the opposition, said:
This motion is not intended in any way by any member as a censure either upon the government or upon any government department. It is simply the desire of those who feel themselves to be the representatives of the taxpayers of the country to get information as to how the taxpayers' money is now being spent, and to get real information in an effective way.
Mr. Bonar Law who, as I have said, was leading the House of Commons, and speaking for the government, is reported as follows:
We feel that the expenditure is so large that even from the point of view of satisfying the country, apart altogether from the House of Commons, that everything is being done to keep it down, it is desirable that further examination by the House of Commons should take place.
It must be clearly understood that reference must be of such a nature as to cut a hard and fast line, if it is possible, an the reference, between criticism of policy and an attempt to control expenditure. That is what we desire.
I propose we should appoint a select committee for two purposes, first of all-I am not attempting to give the exact terms of reference -to consider whether additional control can be obtained and in what way it can best be obtained as a permanent arrangement, and in addition to that we should authorize the same committee to do at once what was done by those cabinet committees of which my right hon. friend spoke, and go into the department to examine the method of expenditure, and make recommendations either to the House of Commons or to the department.
That is my proposal. It is not a shelving motion in any sense, and it only carries out what is certainly my own view, that we ought

War Expenditures-Special Committee
to do something more to satisfy not merely the House of Commons but the country-that we are doing all we can to get value for the money we have spent.
In concluding his statement Mr. Bonar Law used these words:
But if the House of Commons only desires- and I am sure it does-not to appoint a roaming commission to seek out grounds of criticism and attack upon the government-to effect some more real control over the vast expenditure, then that is what is desired by the government also, a.nd my proposal gives it the opportunity.
I think the words of Mr. Bonar Law just quoted are similar to those which I used in this house on December 3 when I said:
... a committee which takes its responsibilities seriously, and will assist the government in exercising a control over the expenditures which are being made, keeping on the government the responsibility for policy, but being free to make suggestions that will be helpful and constructive, should be of the greatest possible service.
After the committee had begun its work the matter was again discussed at different times in the British house. Mr. Herbert Samuel, speaking for the opposition and referring to the work of the committee, made the following statement:
It approaches its investigations not in any spirit of hostility-as the chancellor of the exchequer has very kindly acknowledged-for we recognize, heaven knows, how heavy and how difficult are the tasks of those charged with the duties of administration during this war-[DOT] but in a spirit of what I may call friendly vigilance, and with a single-minded desire to make such practical suggestions as commend themselves to us for effective saving; and in order to promote what is the most essential thing of all, an atmosphere of economy pervading the whole of the spending departments of the state.
Speaking on behalf of the government, and also referring to the work of the committee, Mr. Bonar Law said:
I must say that when the committee was set up, the government not only assented to it, but, I think, welcomed it. It was understood that the object of that committee would be not to harass the government departments, not to worry about mistakes which have been made in the past, except so far as they have a bearing on the future, but to devote themselves to helping the country, if possible, in keeping down the expenditure. I am glad to say that not only from their report, but from all I have heard about this committee, that it is in that spirit they have undertaken their work.
I give those passages to the house as indicating the spirit which governed the committee in its work and as indicating also the nature of the work and its scope. That was in 1917 and 1918. When the present war broke out, the British House of Commons had the experience of that committee to guide it,

7SA
and it had all the discussions that had taken place in the committee as well as the reports. There were members of the British house who had served on that committee and who knew the value of its work. For that reason, when the present committee was proposed in the British house, every one was more or less familiar with its purpose, its method of carrying on its proceedings, its value, and the like. The result was that there was little or no discussion and no division when it came to the appointment of a committee.
May I draw attention to another fact brought out by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. The committee in England was formed when Mr. Chamberlain was still Prime Minister and when, as the leader of the opposition said, there was an opposition party in the British House of Commons. I suppose there will be some who will say, "Oh, well, they have a union or a national government in Great Britain and that makes all the difference." I may deal with that, if necessary, a little later on. I would now point out that when the committee was functioning in 1917 there was an effective opposition, of which Mr. Herbert Samuel was the leader. The opposition in the British house at that time was made up of Liberals and Labour members.
I would also point out that when the present resolution was adopted in the British house it was at a time when the Labour party was in opposition, under Mr. Attlee, Mr. Bevin and other gentlemen. At that time there was in Great Britain no national government in the form in which it is at the present time. I have just been reminded that it was Sir Archibald Sinclair, the leader of the Liberal opposition in the British house, who asked for the appointment of the committee. He was supported by the Labour opposition and the Liberals, and both oppositions were joined by the government in a unanimous agreement to appointing a committee. So far as I have heard or know, there has never been any occasion to challenge the wisdom of the decision that was reached at that time.
I come now to a further reason why we feel it would be desirable to adopt the resolution in the form in which it is. Not only have we the example of the British house to guide us in its terms and method of proceeding, we have the advantage of having before us reports of the committee itself. When the leader of the opposition proposed this committee he said that he had in his hand copies of the reports of the committee which had been appointed. I have here the reports of the select committee on national expenditure. I
1228	COMMONS
War Expenditures-Special Committee
have used the phrase "committee to control national expenditure" because that is the designation used continually throughout the reports. The committee is known as the select committee on national expenditure. I assume that will be the name of this committee to deal with war expenditures.
I should like to go through these reports and indicate to the house what they contain, but that would take considerable time. I shall, however, give to the house from the reports themselves some particulars with respect to the British committee and its work, because this information will serve to indicate the scope of the committee that it is proposed to set up here, and the extent of the work it will have to undertake. I venture to say that hon. members will be amazed when they learn how wide is the latitude which the government has given to private members to investigate matters of expenditure pertaining to the war.
The first report of the committee was dated January 16, 1940. It outlines the organization. The committee of Great Britain had twenty-eight members, and it was divided into seven subcommittees which dealt with the following subjects:
1.	Army services.
2.	Navy services.
3.	Air services.
4.	Supply services.
5.	Home defence services.
6.	Trade, agriculture and economic warfare.
7.	A coordinating subcommittee composed of the chairman of the whole committee and the chairman of each subcommittee.
I intend to read two or three paragraphs of the proceedings of the committee in Great Britain because I think they will throw a little light upon the nature of the proceedings and possibly guide our committee when it undertakes its duties.
The second report points out that the committee "conceive it to be more their duty to prevent or check waste before it occurs than to conduct enquiries into past events." At this stage four more members had been added to the committee and an additional subcommittee on transport services had been set up. The subjects upon which specific recommendations were made in this report were:
1.	The coordination of procedure in the letting of government contracts.
2.	The design, specification and supply of
warlike stores with a view:	(a) to get, if
possible, -an equally serviceable article at lower cost; (b) to get an equally serviceable article with quicker delivery; (c) to ensure that specifications include no superfluous quantities, qualities, or frills; (d) to exclude imported
{Mr. Mackenzie King.]
materials which are not essential; (e) to exclude domestic materials of which the supply is short.
3.	The building programme.
4.	The selection of sites for government buildings.
5.	Competitive bidding for skilled workmen.
6.	The consideration of the prevention of waste and salvage by a fact-finding survey.
In connection with the committee's report I have noted this particular paragraph which I think is of interest:
The efficacy of your committee's investigations will perhaps never be fully obvious, either to the house or to the public at large, from their published reports alone. Not only do considerations of public interest preclude them from stating certain facts and figures, but also it has been found that the investigations themselves have led to immediate action by departments which might normally not have been taken till a formal report of the committee had been brought to their notice. Sufficient instances of this kind have occurred to convince your committee that this is one of the most valuable results of their activities, since their discovery of waste, actual or potential, brings immediate action with a view to its removal. This prompt contribution to efficiency and economy is, your committee submit, more vital to the national interest than the formulation of reports of a sensational or spectacular character.
The third report is an amended report from the subcommittee on army services. The subcommittee had, by April 10, 1940, held twenty meetings and heard twenty-eight witnesses. One of the chief subjects of inquiry was the army programme of building. The committee found that the necessity of speed in camp construction had inflated costs both of materials and of labour.
I wish to make clear to the house that the committees investigating these matters have gone very thoroughly into their work and have not hesitated to make very clear, where-ever they found evidence of wasteful expenditure, just what the circumstances were. Here is one case and I give it as an instance because I have heard others commenting on the existence of similar situations here. The committee also found that not enough attention had been given to using small contractors in this work of camp construction and that delays which might have been avoided had existed in making plans available to contractors.
The committee also found deficiencies in the army methods of requisitioning land and buildings for military use.
The fourth report dealt with trade, agriculture and economic warfare. I do not know that I need to go into the details of that.

War Expenditures-Special Committee
The fifth report dealt with air services. Here I pause to give the house a reference to the contents of that report:
The report is not concerned with the general activities of the Air Ministry but with two particular matters:	(1) the site of a repair
depot in Scotland and (2) an aerodrome in Kent.
Following the fifth report, the committee issued a special report, on May 28, 1940, dealing with its own procedure.
I shall take occasion to refer to this special report when I have concluded what I have to say about the other reports, 'because it contains mention of some things which I think will be helpful to hon. members in appreciating considerations of which full account must be taken.
The sixth report deals with the subcommittee on supply services and goes into questions of specifications of supplies; coordination of purchases; overtime for labour; salvage of waste products; the extension of the field of production through using all possible firms, large and small, for government orders.
The seventh report deals with the subcommittee on navy services. This report is concerned with the letting of contracts, the repair and construction of ships, and Sunday work on ship repairs.
The eighth report deals with home defence services.
The ninth report deals with transport services; the tenth report with priority organization; the eleventh report with replies of the departments to the first eight reports of the committee; the twelfth report with army services, and the thirteenth report with government films.
So far as I can learn, when the British house adjourned, the committee ceased to function but was reappointed as soon as the house reassembled on November 26. Before November 26, the committee had prepared one further report, the fourteenth. I have not been able to get the actual report itself. The fourteenth report was made on October 15, 1940. The committee, which was reconstituted at the beginning of the new session on November 26, issued its third report in January. This report dealt with labour waste in contracts and was reviewed by the parliamentary correspondent of the London Times on January 16.
I have not thus far been able to secure any other report, but what I have read, Mr. Speaker, indicates the very wide scope of activity for such a committee and will let members of the house see the nature of the service which it is possible to render to
the government in assisting to control expenditures, to avoid waste and to prevent misdoing of any kind in connection with government contracts.
The special report of the committee was clearly made with a view to giving to the British house and to the public information which the committee felt it was important for the house to have in time of war. I quote from this special report:
1.	Your committee concluded their second report by observing that the efficacy of their investigations might never be fully obvious from their published reports alone. In some cases, as they pointed out, their investigations had led to immediate action by the departments -a result which renders formal recommendations unnecessary-and in other cases they were precluded from stating certain facts and figures by considerations of public interest.
2.	Your committee feel bound to revert to the difficulty caused, in time of war, by considerations of the latter kind, in that they inevitably hamper the procedure of reporting to the house. In normal times, a select committee discharge their duty by reporting their views to the house, usually with the evidence on which these views are based. The order of the house for the printing of the report and the evidence (if reported) is presumed to have been made as a matter of course, and publication duly ensues. On this the house, whether or no a formal debate takes place, can form its own judgment. In time of war this unrestricted publicity is incompatible with considerations of public interest, since nothing can be safely published which would give valuable information to the enemy. The difficulty, therefore, with which your committee is faced is how to fulfil their duty of reporting criticisms of departmental action or disagreements with departmental views, when the publication of their findings might endanger national security.
3.	Your committee find themselves in this dilemma: considerations of national safety may preclude them from publishing certain recommendations and the arguments on which they are based, while the normal practice of the house prevents them from communicating their report to the members of the war cabinet who alone can take executive action to compel the departments to adopt your committee's recommendations. They feel bound to inform the house that, in order to carry out the task imposed upon them, the chairman of the committee and the chairmen of subcommittees, with the authorization of the committee or of the subcommittee in question, have considered it essential to approach ministers for direct discussions on matters arising from their inquiries and on the advisability of publicly stating certain facts and figures. This method of informal approach, however, though highly valuable, does not solve the whole problem.
4.	Your committee are mindful that their duty is to the house. But, in war, the supreme consideration is to secure efficiency and swiftness in executive action, while preventing the disclosure of vital facts. Procedure must be moulded to fit these circumstances.
5.	Your committee, therefore, recommend that when, in their opinion, a report should not be presented, their coordinating subcommittee
1230	COMMONS
War Expenditures-Special Committee
(which consists of the chairman of the committee and the chairmen of the subcommittees) should be empowered to address a memorandum to the Prime Minister for the consideration of the war cabinet, with a request for a considered reply thereto; and that your committee do report to the house on every occasion when this power shall have been exercised. They ask the house to give them this power.
In making these quotations I do not wish for a moment to have it assumed that the government proposes to put any restrictions on the committee that is appointed beyond those that are set forth in the terms of reference itself. But I feel it is only right and fair that at this stage, so that there may be no doubt hereafter as to whether or not a wise course is being pursued, that I should bring to the attention of the house some of the reasons why the British committee, when it was appointed, proceeded in the manner in which it did. I took occasion a day or two ago to telegraph to the high commissioner to ascertain whether what I had gathered from its own reports, namely, that the proceedings of the British committee had been for the most part in camera was correct or not. His reply to me was that the committees in England have held their proceedings in camera.
I can see at once wherein that circumstance is capable of being grossly misconstrued. Someone may say, "Well, we do not do business in that way as a rule." Of course we do not as a rule; but what I wish to emphasize to this house is what Mr. Churchill himself has had to emphasize over and over in the British parliament, namely, that we are now at war, and that things which can be done in certain ways in peace time cannot always with wisdom be proceeded with in the same manner in a time of war.
I have in my hand the report of the debate that took place in the British House of Commons on the 27th of last month. Hon. members will no doubt have noticed it. It was a debate that arose out of the appointment of the Right Hon. Malcolm MacDonald as high commissioner to Canada. The government had introduced a bill to permit members who received appointments from the government in connection with the war effort to retain their seats in parliament. Sir Samuel Hoare, Sir Stafford Cripps, who was at Moscow, and one or two others had received appointments and would in the nature of things have vacated their seats but tor the special act that wias being passed. Mr. Churchill said that he felt that in a time of war it was absolutely necessary' that the ministry should have the right to make certain appointments from among members in the house, and lie added that he would regard any vote against his motion as a vote of
rMr. Mackenzie King.]
want of confidence in his government. I do not propose to take such a stand in this parliament, but what I wish particularly to direct attention to is what appears to have taken place in the debate to which I have referred. Let me read from the dispatch;
In the same session Mr. Churchill, declaring impatiently that "I really must emphasize that there is a war on," turned down a request for a debate on the leasing of western hemisphere defence bases to the United States.
There, surely, was an apparently innocent enough subject for the House of Commons to discuss, one in which the British public was vitally interested-the leasing of certain British property to the United States. Yet Mr. Churchill would not allow a debate to take place on that subject in the British house, where members are so careful to have their property and other rights fully respected.
Why did Mr. Churchill not wish to have that debate? Because he knew that the minute a debate took place it might disclose in the House of Commons a difference of view which would be a great comfort to the enemy and might sow seeds of difficulty between Great Britain and the United States. He said, therefore, that in this time of war, when the nation is struggling to preserve the security of the state, this being its first consideration, he could not allow a debate to arise upon a question of that kind.
It is for similar reasons that in matters that involve the disclosure of facts, figures, as would give rise to situations which would be of aid or comfort to the enemy, it has been thought desirable to have these committees proceed in the way in which their own best judgment dictates. That is the reason. It is not that the government has anything to hide, or wishes to hide anything. It is because in a time of war, knowing the great responsibilities that rest upon the ministry and that the ministry must retain the confidence of the country if its war effort is to succeed, that this procedure is necessary. I say that without any hesitation. If confidence in the government is undermined or destroyed, that is going to have its effect upon the war effort of the country. Let the House of Commons give its confidence to the government or withhold it; but so long as we have the confidence of parliament, let us carry on our war effort in the best way we possibly can. If there is any reason why we should lose that confidence, let the reason be stated. But in the meantime I suggest, in the interests of what is best for the country in a time of war, that it is

War Expenditures-Special Committee
desirable that confidence in government should be maintained in the eyes of the people.
May I come now to what I said of an effort being made to create the impression that the government has something to hide or is seeking to conceal something. That reason was put forward by my hon. friend, not as his belief but as the way in which many people would interpret the resolution if the word "current" were left in, the committee being appointed to examine current expenditure defrayed out of public moneys. Leaving in the word "current" might make it appear that the government was trying to hide something that had been done in the past which was not covered by current expenditure.

speechtext:
If that was not
the reason, a section of the press has not been slow in trying to have it appear that there is some reason of the kind existing. I have in my hand an editorial that appeared in the Montreal Gazette of March 1. The leader of the opposition a day or two ago advised members of the house not to attempt to enter into controversy with the press; he said that whoever took that task upon himself might expect the press to have the last word and would fare worse in the end. As a member of parliament, I feel that the rights of parliament are supreme over the press or any other institution in the country; and if I find the press of the country misrepresenting the position as it affects the government or its war effort, I intend to take exception most emphatically to what the press says. The press is one power in the country, but I hope the day will never come when the press supplants the place that parliament is supposed to have in upholding the rights of the people. There is one other power that is supreme over press and parliament alike, namely, the people of the country; and the people of this country, on more than one occasion, have shown what they feel with respect to a press that represents a point of view contrary to that which they themselves entertain.
May I read a part of this editorial dated March 1. I would have the house keep in mind that February 19 was the date on which
it was agreed between the leader of the opposition and myself that the word "current" would be dropped out of the resolution and that the resolution that I would submit to the house would be to appoint a committee to examine expenditures defrayed out of public moneys, without any limitation by the word "current." The resolution having appeared on the order paper, the Montreal Gazette of March 1 said editorially:
The wording is significant inasmuch as it binds the committee in advance by whatever construction the government may put upon the words "consistent with the execution of the policy."
That is the first effort to undermine confidence in the purpose of the administration in submitting this resolution in the form in which it is, including the words "consistent with the execution of the policy." My first answer to that criticism is that these words appear in the resolution of the British House of Commons in the order to its committee. But they appear there, and they appear here for the reason that the government is responsible to parliament for policy, and no committee of the House of Commons has the right under any procedure known to parliament to intervene between parliament and the administration. The question of policy is a question for the government to decide, a question to be debated on the floor of the house. It is not the business of a committee appointed by the house to decide whether policy is correct or incorrect; that can be discussed between the government and hon. members on the floor of the house.
But the editorial goes on:
The phrase is restrictive, and as such it reveals a disinclination on the part of the government to allow the committee the free scope which some of its members may deem desirable and even necessary in the public interest. If the work of the committee is to be directed in accordance with the interest of the government if and whenever that interest appears to be in conflict with the interest of the taxpayer and of the national war effort, it follows that the results must be incomplete and therefore unsatisfactory.
Is that fair comment? Could anything be more unfair than that, for a responsible journal to challenge the intent and purpose and motives of the government in giving members of the House of Commons the right to investigate to the extent this motion does, in saying, "if the work is to be in the interest of the government"? I wish it to be understood that the work of this committee is to be, and I believe it will be, in the interest of the public and in no other interest. The government is here to serve the public interest and is asking for this committee to help in that effort.

War Expenditures-Special Committee
The editorial goes on:
Unfortunately, there is other evidence justifying an apprehension as to the government's attitude.
Notice that word "evidence". There is "other evidence". We have not had any evidence thus far. No evidence has been adduced up to the present, only misrepresentation, unfair comment. But:
Unfortunately, there is other evidence justifying an apprehension as to the government's attitude.
This in a time of war when we are told that the Conservative party-and this paper certainly represents what is left of the Conservative party-is trying to cooperate with the government in the matter of Canada's war effort. Note this following sentence:
The scope of the committee's labours was discussed on Monday between the Prime Minister, the leader of the opposition and some of the latter's colleagues, and reports from Ottawa are that the deliberations were not amicable.
That reference is to Monday, February 24. It was on February 19 that a decision was reached to omit the word "current" from the resolution. The meeting of the 24th dealt with a still further enlargement of this proposal, but it did not alter that question of the agreement of the government to allow the word "current" to come out.
The editorial continues:
They were, on the contrary, heated and acrimonious, assuming the correctness of information obtained by the Canadian Press. The substance of the story is that opposition members tried to insist upon the committee's right to examine all war expenditures incurred since the commencement of the conflict whereas the Prime Minister was prepared only to permit examination of current outlays as is done in Britain. The Conservative retort was that the British committee has been at work since the war began and therefore has knowledge of all expenditures and what was got for them.
I leave hon. members to reach their own conclusion as to where the Gazette got its inspiration. Certainly it was not from anyone on this side of the house.

The three hon. members who were present at the conference have all spoken and I accept their word, that not one of them gave any kind of intimation of what took place at the conference to any member of the press. I say the same with respect to all my colleagues who were present. Nevertheless, we get this interesting account. Perhaps there was an intermediary. Let me read a little further.
The inference is that Mr. King is afraid of a full investigation.
All this is based on the assertion that I would not allow the word "current" to go out. And I had stricken it out ten days before. It goes on:
Rightly or wrongly, that is how his position will be interpreted by the people of Canada. They will conclude that he has something to hide and they will have ground for believing that it is something exceedingly grave.
And this is interesting:
This ground is supplied in the amazing statement that the Prime Minister threatened to resign if he could not have his way. Surely this country, at this time of all times, is entitled to something better from the head of its government than the behaviour of a temperamental prima donna.
I think this is the first time, it is as far as I am aware, that I have been credited with being a temperamental prima donna. I rather thought the criticism was that I was far too colourless, that I did not give the press anything for headlines, that I was not spectacular enough, that I did not say nasty things about other people and gain special prominence for so doing. Then it goes on to say:
This is not war leadership, if it is leadership at all, and the greatest war in history is reaching its most critical stage, as critical for Canada as for any other country. The whole situation in regard to this war expenditure committee looks wrong, about as wrong as it could be. and it leaves a very bad taste in the mouth of the public.
I ask hon. members if that is fair criticism. Are not all these not only false insinuations but false statements? Are they not malicious statements? I go so far as to say that that article is libellous; first, because it is false, and, second, because it is malicious, and it bears the stigma of both these things on its face. I go further and say it infringes the privileges of this house.

War Expenditures-Special Committee
I come now to another paper. Just before six o'clock I read to the house how strongly the Toronto Globe and Mail eulogized the administration for its stand before adjournment in agreeing to accept the motion put forward at the suggestion of the leader of the opposition, and for undertaking to introduce the motion being put forward to-day. But what is said in an article that appears in the Globe and Mail to-day on the same resolution? Hon. members will notice that these articles have been appearing before the subject matter has been discussed in this house. In other words, fill the public mind with all the prejudice you possibly can before there is any opportunity for the government to say a word, and then in the next editorial say that the government found itself on the defensive and that Mr. King spent most of the afternoon trying to defend himself against some accusations that he must know are only too true.
The editorial I read just before recess was headed something about confidence being established. This one is headed "The First Billion Dollars." It not only misrepresents motives as the editorial I have read from the Montreal Gazette did, but it also misrepresents the facts. It begins, by speaking of:
. . the reported determination of the Prime Minister to prevent examination of the first billion dollars spent on the war.
In other words, leading the public to assume that I am preventing inquiry into "the first billion dollars", being the first year's war expenditure. It goes on to say that I have precluded the committee on public accounts from meeting, and goes on to say:
The right of the public accounts committee to examine the accounts of the past year has been recognized for more than half a century.
It quotes at length from Sir Richard Cartwright, Sir John Thompson and others to show that the public accounts committee have a perfect right to examine accounts relating to the past, and it leaves the impression that I have been and am preventing the public accounts committee from meeting and am also determined to prevent this committee from going into the public expenditure for more than a year.
What are the facts about the public accounts committee? The committee was set up in this house on November 22, if I am not mistaken.
The committee is there; it can meet at any time any Iron, member wishes to have it called. The auditor general's report was tabled in this house, I have forgotten on what date. If it has not been referred to the
committee on public accounts, that has been due to an oversight, and I would ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) to see that it is referred to the committee to-morrow. The public accounts committee is there, as it always has been, and this government is not trying in any way to prevent that committee from functioning, going into any matter into which it may wish to inquire. Any hon. member has the right to request that this should be done. But let me read the conclusion of this editorial:
Ministers may argue speciously that rules which might apply to the regular public accounts committee of the commons and be faithfully observed in its proceedings are not applicable to a special committee on war expenditures, but the argument will not hold water. It is no credit to governments or parliaments that the public accounts committee has not functioned for years, but the special committee on war expenditures has under the strong pressure of public opinion been conceded by the government as a substitute for it in order that popular disquietude about certain features of the ministry's war programme might be allayed.
I say that statement is an entire falsehood. The committee which is being set up, if this house accepts this resolution, is not in substitution for the public accounts committee; it is in addition to the public accounts committee. This is a committee that can go back over ground which should be confined to the public accounts committee, and which in Great Britain is so confined. Then the editorial concludes:
It will be farcical and something wo-rse if the government, having conceded the committee, reduces it to partial impotence by debarring it from inquiring into the first billion dollars of expenditures, and the opposition will be derelict in its duty if it does not insist upon the withdrawal of any limitations upon the investigation.
I do not think I need say more about that article. Why are these editorials put forward at this time? When the opposition in this house profess that they are cooperating with the government, seeking to help in the war effort; when they are being praised by the Montreal Gazette and the Toronto Globe and Mail for that patriotic attitude, why do these papers attack this administration, not on anything we have done but accusing us of something we have not done and have never thought of doing, and then condemn us on that specious charge? If that is cooperating in war effort, I have still to learn the meaning of the word "cooperation."
I am not going to take the time of the house to go over other press comments, but there is one with which I wish to deal 'because it reflects on every member of this house.

War Expenditures-Special Committee
Before I do so, I think I might read to hon. members one or two citations from "Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms," relating to the privileges of members of this house. Citation 157, under standing order 16, reads:
Interference with or reflections upon members have been resented as indignities to the house itself.
Then citation 162:
Scandalous charges or imputations directed against members of a select committee are equivalent to libellous charges brought against the house itself, while a letter complaining that a member who had been nominated upon a select committee would be unable to act impartially upon it has been adjudged a breach of privilege.
I think the sooner it is understood both inside and outside this house that any charge that members being appointed to committees of this house cannot act impartially is a breach of the privileges of this house, the better it will be. Any charge of partiality, or assumption of partiality, on the part of a member of the house serving on a committee is a reflection upon the member and also upon- the house itself; and, as the one who is more responsible than any other in this house for maintaining the rights of members and the privileges of the house, it is part of my duty to bring that matter prominently at this time to the attention of hon. members and of some of those who control the press in the country. I find as the heading of an article which appears in the Toronto Globe and Mail of February 22, 1941, "Impartial Probe Desirable." T-hen I read this statement:
In another column on this page we publish a pertinent letter from Mr. Harry R. Jackman, M.P. for Toronto-Rosed-ale, in which he makes the point that the maximum effectiveness of the special parliamentary committee on national expenditures is not likely to result unless there is on the committee adequate -representation of the opposition.
I have before me the letter referred to; I shall not read it. The hon. gentleman is one of the new members of the house, and I am prepared to believe that he wrote the letter without realizing the extent to which it reflected upon every member of this house. I will go on and read what is said in this editorial appearing in the Globe and Mail:
It is not -to be expected that the ten Liberal members will bestir themselves to expose the shortcomings of the government; consequently the task of ferreting out information will devolve upon the handful of Conservative and leftist members.
This editorial is a reflection upon every hon. gentleman on this side of the house, without exception, and is a reflection upon this house itself.

Yes; I am prepared to give them a certificate of credit with respect to the integrity with which they are bound to and will, I believe, discharge their duties.
There is one word with which I should like to conclude. In the course of our conversations together, the leader of the opposition asked me if I would give him, in the form of a memorandum, what I had said to him I felt to be an essential consideration in connection with the appointment of the committee. I sent my hon. friend the memorandum he requested, in the form of a letter, and I believe he will take no exception to my reading the letter to the house because it expresses what I believe ought to be present to the mind of each hon. member who serves on the committee, and in fact to the mind of every hon. member in the house.
In these days, when one has reason to know a good deal about the possible trend of the world situation, when one faces from hour to hour the possibiltiy of having to make some announcement to the house about a development which will fill the minds of all with immediate concern, it is not an easy burden, may I say, to have one's motives continually misrepresented! to the public as being those of a person who is considering only what he can hide or what he can conceal, a person having ulterior motives in everything he does. I believe I have been long enough in this House of Commons for hon. members to know where I stand on questions of public integrity.
