speechtext:
I believe, too, that I can let my life record speak for itself in that regard. But if I say to this House
14873-79}
of Commons that there are some considerations which make it impossible to-day, in a time of war, to proceed as we would ordinarily proceed in times of peace, I hope it will be understood that I have the very best of reasons for so saying. I do not think I need to state them for hon. members to appreciate their importance. It is not only Canada's war effort that is at stake in this war. Anything which affects adversely Canada's war effort is going to affect adversely the war effort of the British empire. It is going to do more than that; it is going to affect adversely the war effort of all those forces fighting for freedom against tyranny, against world domination.
I have striven as best I could to prevent things from being said in this House of Commons which might make us responsible for some aspect of the war for which none of us would care to be responsible. I have been chided for that. I have been chided because I have said, "Let us be careful what we say here. It may not be understood in other countries in the way it is understood here." But at least my conscience is clear in that I have uttered no word I know of which could provoke any situation, or make a bad situation worse. I believe I am equally clear in my own conscience when I say that I have asked nothing of this House of Commons from any motive other than that of what I considered to be most necessary to make our war effort as effective as possible, and to prevent anything from happening which might at a time of crisis make a bad situation worse.
It was that which I had in mind when I sent this letter to my hon. friend, in answer to his request. Upon reading the letter I shall have concluded what I wish to say. It is as follows:
Ottawa, February 20, 1941 The Honourable R. B. Hanson, P.C., M.P.,
Leader of the Opposition,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Hanson:
You have asked me to let you have, in the form of a memorandum, the consideration of which I mentioned full account should be taken in the terms of reference of the committee on national expenditure.
In a word, what I mentioned was that I thought the United Kingdom was as concerned about the control of expenditures in time of war as Canada; that unquestionably the government and parliament of the United Kingdom had considered the matter from every possible angle, and that I thought there must have been the best of reasons for the terms of reference of the select committee of the British House of Commons being in the words they are, both as regards what they contain and what they do not contain.
I suggested -that, having read the reports of the United Kingdom select committee on national expenditure, you yourself would be
War Expenditures-Special

Committee
wholly familiar with the reasons which, at a time of war, had caused the British parliament to proceed with respect to national expenditures in the manner it had, and that I hoped you might find it possible to explain these reasons to members of your party who might be conferring with you concerning the terms of reference of the committee to be appointed by our own House of Commons.
The war effort of the British commonwealth of nations is a united effort. Whatever affects that effort in one part has its effect upon all. I should feel I was assuming a very grave responsibility if, in a matter to which the United Kingdom parliament had given every consideration, and had adopted a procedure respecting national expenditures which it deemed imperative at a time of war, I were not to point out to all concerned the responsibility which our own House of Commons would be taking upon itself in departing from the procedure followed at Westminster, particularly where that procedure had been adopted with special reference to war-time expenditures.
You will have observed that the select committee on national expenditure of the British House of Commons drew the attention of the house in a special report to the difficulties caused by considerations of public interest in following ordinary procedure in time of war.
The following appears in the report of the committee:
"In normal times, a select committee discharge their duty by reporting their views to the house, usually with the evidence on which the views are based. The order of the house for the printing of the report and the evidence -if reported-is presumed to have been made as a matter of course, and publication duly ensues. On this the house, whether or no a formal debate takes place, can form its own judgment. In time of war this unrestricted publicity is incompatible with considerations of public interest, since nothing can be safely published which would give valuable information to the enemy."
Another section of the same report is as follows:
"Your committee are mindful that their duty is to the house. But, in war, the supreme consideration is to secure efficiency and swiftness in executive action, while preventing the disclosure of vital facts. Procedure must be moulded to fit these circumstances."
It was these aspects of the matter which I felt placed a responsibility upon every party and member in the House of Commons, not less than upon the government, and which I was anxious, as leader of the opposition, you should have particularly in mind.
You will, no doubt, recollect that these were matters carefully considered at a conference which was held in my office prior to adjournment, at which the question of the nature of the committee to be appointed to deal with national expenditures was considered between yourself, Mr. Stirling and Mr. Green and some of my colleagues and myself.
Yours sincerely.
W. L. Mackenzie King.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure we
have all listened with the most intense interest to the two-hour address of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) which he has just concluded. I confess I am surprised that he took so much time to defend a position which, so far as I am aware, has not been the subject of intense attack at least by us on this side of the house, whatever it may have been in the country.
I am bound to say that the first impressions on my mind are that he has proved, beyond peradventure, the value of the suggestion which I made to the house and the country on December 3. Second, he has taken the opportunity to battle with his friends the press in connection with the attitude they have taken with regard to this subject. May I say that so far as his engaging in that combat is concerned, I leave him to his friends of the press. They are quite able to take care of themselves, and no one has asked me to constitute myself as their champion.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is just as well.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Further,
I should like to say that never at any time have I communicated to the press any of the proceedings of the confidential conferences that were held from time to time with regard to this matter. I have been amazed at the crossing of wires which seems to have occurred and at the stories which have been published in the press with respect to what is thought to have taken place. I will just say to them that they appear to have mixed up two things. I am going to leave that matter right there.
At the risk of taking a little time-I promise the house that I shall not take up one-half the time taken by the Prime Minister-I should like to take the house back to the date when I first brought up the question of the examination of war expenditures. Speaking in the debate on the address on November 12, 1940, I made the following observations, which were referred to in part by the Prime Minister, and which will be found at page 34 of Hansard:
We on your left, sir, hold the view, and I believe it is well founded, that it has been the deliberate policy of the government, during the past session as well as during the interval since we adjourned in August, to endeavour to create the impression that all was well with our war effort. In our view the government has sought to lull and soothe the Canadian people into a false sense of security, and continues to do so. It has sought to convince the people that we are living in the best of all possible worlds.

War Expenditures-Special Committee
Those who are alive to the situation know the clangers that lurk behind such a position, and they are alike alarmed and anxious. Knowing of this feeling, I am impelled to propose to the government that it cause to be set up immediately two select special committees which will be charged with the responsibility and the duty of investigating and reporting to this house factually, objectively and truthfully, without bias and without partisanship-and I have no doubt that is possible-what is our exact position (a) with respect to our fighting forces, military, naval and air; and (b) with respect to the production and delivery of all the important materials, equipment and supplies necessary in our war effort, so that the Canadian people may know the truth. Before such committees ministers could appear and be subject to questioning. Progress reports in the form of speeches in the house by ministers are not good enough. You can never elicit the naked facts in that manner. Only the time-proven method of cross-examination by question and answer will suffice. The process should be free from anything in the nature of propaganda. The public has been fed that until it is nauseated.
Then I go on to say;
The government may hold the view that it is not in the public interest that the facts and figures for which I am asking be disclosed. I know the matter is not free from difficulties. When I make the proposal I visualize many of its implications, but I am convinced that the method I have suggested is the only real way in which the government may satisfy the public. I am willing with some of my colleagues to meet with the Prime Minister and some of his colleagues so that we may consider the whole proposal, in an honest effort to arrive at a conclusion.
That was the proposal which I laid before this House of Commons on November 12 last. That proposal related to two distinct matters, namely, an investigation into the armed forces of the nation and one into production and expenditure. In ordinary peace times I would never have made any such suggestion; in ordinary peace times it would not have been necessary; in ordinary peace times there would be available the usual procedure and methods to investigate these matters. But because we were at war, because there was- questioning in the hearts and minds of the Canadian people as to the * government's war effort, I thought this should be done. Why should there not be such questioning? I am not going to traverse with respect to this matter the ground I have covered on previous occasions.
The Prime Minister knows the charges made against his government with regard to the war effort during the first twelve months of this war just as well as I do. The fact that the charges are true is why we are so far behind to-day after eighteen months of war. I am not, however, going into that matter to-night. I felt impelled to make that request of the Prime Minister because this
nation was at war, and I think I made it in reasonably moderate language. At all events no exception was taken to the manner or the method that I suggested. I suggested a conference and the Prime Minister was good enough to give it to me. We met, and I am bound to say that my understanding was that at the conference we agreed that it would be confidential in nature. I understood that we were to speak freely, and I tried to observe that from A to Z. We did speak freely.
I did not go into details of what I had said in the house, because the Prime Minister and his colleagues knew that without my telling them. My colleagues knew it without my speaking about it. I do not intend to go into the details of my conversation with the members of the government, but I will say that the government would not accept the proposals which I made. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) gave the reasons for not accepting one proposal. I shall not go into those reasons, but I want to be quite frank in what I say. The Minister of National Defence stated that in a time of war it would be impossible for his headquarters' staff to be at the beck and call of a parliamentary committee. I am bound to tell the house that I agreed with him. That was the spirit in which I met them. I shall not elaborate on that statement, but if he desires to do so he is at liberty. I shall free him from anything. I was impressed with his statement as to the undesirability at this critical time of having his officers delegated to wait upon a parliamentary committee appointed to investigate the position of outfighting forces, military, naval and air.
With regard to the investigation of questions relating to the production and delivery of all the important materials, equipment and supplies necessary in our war effort, there was not so much unanimity. I could not get the consent of the government to investigate those matters. Until last week the attitude of the government with respect to giving information relating to the production of equipment and supplies was quite apparent. We have been deluged with promises and expectations, but we have been told nothing factually as to what the government's effort was in terms of production and delivery. We never got that until the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) gave it to us last week in connection with the war appropriation measure. The government had taken that attitude and I had no power to compel them to do otherwise. I did not try to compel them after that conference. We failed in our

War Expenditures-Special Committee
initial undertaking, but that initial undertaking was made in the utmost good faith in an effort to ascertain for the Canadian people just what this government had been doing along the lines of the two subject matters involved in the suggestion that I made. We failed in that, and for that failure I am sure the Prime Minister will assume responsibility. He has already anticipated criticism here to-night in that regard.
Having failed in that direction, I turned the matter over in my mind. I still felt that something ought to be done; if I could not get a full measure of the story that ought to be told the Canadian people, I thought that possibly I could get something like a halfway measure, and therefore I did not let the matter die. On December 3, having heard what had taken place in England, I came back to this house, and in the course of a debate I made a proposal which will be found at page 615 of Hansard. At the risk of wearying the house, but in order that it may be on the record, I propose to read what I said on that occasion with regard to this matter. I quote:
Speaking on a former occasion I requested specifically that parliament be informed as to what results had been attained with respect to production and deliveries, because we held the view, and I believe it is well founded, that it was the deliberate policy of the government, during the past session as well as during the interval since we adjourned in August, to endeavour to create, by general statements of what we are going to do in the future, the impression that all was well with our war effort in the way of production and deliveries.
Then I went on to say:
Therefore I felt impelled to ask the government that it cause to be set up immediately two select special committees, charged with the responsibility and the duty of investigating and reporting to this house, factually, objectively and truthfully, without bias and without partisanship, what our exact position is to-day (a) with respect to our fighting forces, military, naval and air, and (b) with respect to the production and delivery of all the important materials, equipment and supplies necessary to our war effort, so that the Canadian people might know the truth.
There was no suggestion of scandal there. What I was asking for was facts, information- information which I declared the Canadian people were entitled to get and which up to that time had been specifically denied them. That was the position I took on the first occasion, and it was the position I reiterated on December 3. Then I went on to say:
So far, such committees have not been set up. I indicated that I knew there were difficulties, and I would ask the Prime Minister, if he can and will, to tell the house what the attitude of the government is with respect to that.

I knew what the attitude of the government was with respect to it. They had told us, and in my own mind I had practically abandoned the effort which I had undertaken and the objective I had in view, namely, the whole or one hundred per cent of what I asked for. But I had not abandoned the idea that the Canadian people should be taken into the confidence of the government, to some degree at all events; and I never shall. War time or no war time, the people who are paying the taxes to the government are entitled prima facie to know what is being done with their money, and there are just two restrictions on that. These are, that the safety of the state shall not be endangered by reason of the divulging of such information, and that no aid or comfort to the enemy shall thereby be given. Save for these two limitations, there is no valid reason in the world why the Canadian people should not know what is being done with the money wrung from them by taxation and lent by them to the government.
After all, a point was made by the lady member of the house to-day, that the government of the country are not our rulers but our servants. Do not let us for a moment forget that. I think the Prime Minister, flushed as he is with the result of the voting on March 26 last, has forgotten for the moment that he is the servant of the Canadian people; and if he is not in actual name a dictator, he is rapidly approaching that point of view. Make no mistake about that; the government of this country in war time as in peace time is still, under our democratic system, the servant of the people. Do not let this government get away from that point of view for one instant. As far as I am concerned I intend to iterate and reiterate that point of view.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is a long way from it now.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am afraid we have departed a long way from that principle. Having in mind what had occurred, knowing the attitude of the government, and being impressed, as I said before, with the reasons advanced by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) responsible for the conduct of his staff, responsible for their time and labours, and their direction of our war effort, I realized it was impossible to get the government to accede to the request I had made. I yielded readily on the one point; I did not yield as readily on the other point; and so I turned the matter over in my mind. I had read about what is being done in England. The Prime Minister has indicated to-day

War Expenditures-Special Committee
that this was not a new thing in 1938 when the present committee was set up over there, that it went back as far as 1917. That is a matter of historical interest; it does not add to the value of the thing at the moment.
He said that such a thing was never suggested in Canada before. The Prime Minister was not in parliament in 1917; neither was I. He was not here in 1915; neither was I. But there was a war on in 1915. Sir Robert Borden was Prime Minister, and there was the greatest drive that this country has ever seen against the government of that day in connection with war contracts. What we have attempted to do here is a pacifist movement compared with what Prank Carvell and others did in 1915. What did Sir Robert Borden do? Did he give a limited liability committee? If hon. gentlemen are interested in the historical aspect of this matter, to which the Prime Minister has adverted, I would suggest that they look up Sir Robert Borden's Memoirs, which have had' a great interest for me. Certain expenditures had been made with respect to the purchase of arms and munitions, implements and materials and other supplies for the purpose of the war, and they were being questioned by the then opposition; and in June, 1915, Sir Robert Borden, as stated in his Memoirs, page 492, thought it-
. . . desirable and necessary to establish a commission for the investigation of purchases by the government during the ten months which had elapsed since the outbreak of war.
That goes far beyond anything I have ever asked to have done. These purchases had been quite considerable and the expenditures were investigated by the public accounts committee, but it seemed expedient to continue and enlarge the investigation. What did he do? He appointed Sir Charles Davidson, retired chief justice of the supreme court of Quebec, on June 2, 1915, as a commissioner-what for?
To inquire into, investigate and report upon the purchase, by and on behalf of the government of Canada, through whatever agency the purchases may have been effected, of arms and munitions, implements, materials . . . etc. . . . for the purpose of the present war and as to the expenditures and payments made or agreed to be made therefor.
That is what Sir Robert Borden did, and that went far beyond anything the British government has ever done. That went far beyond anything that this government is now offering to do or even asking us to do. I hold in my hand a copy of order in council, P.C. 1287, approved by His Royal Highness the Governor General on the 2nd day of June, 1915, setting out the scope of the proposed commission, and it is as wide as language can make it. There were no restrictions.
Following the passage of that order in council, a royal commission was issued to Sir Charles Davidson under the provisions of the Inquiries Act. Not only that but the government appointed at public expense eminent counsel to carry on an investigation on behalf of the public or any member of the public who wanted to make a single appearance before that commission on any matter of war expenditures. In other words, Sir Robert Borden opened the door wide to anybody who wanted to walk in. He was not afraid of public opinion. He was not afraid of any breach of privilege. He was not afraid of the Canadian people. They did walk in; the inquiry was held, and evidence was taken under oath. Eminent counsel were appointed; the commission made its report, and as a result of that report certain people were punished. That was something new in the constitutional history of Canada.
When my right hon. friend attempts to convince the people of Canada that what he is accepting or proposing to do is something new or something that is important, I say to him that he had better read his history over again. I say it is not new and it is not nearly as important as what Sir Robert Borden did. Sir Robert Borden followed the proper course. It was the course I failed to convince the Prime Minister in my first conversation with him, based on the statement I made on the 12th of November, should be adopted. I would not have mentioned that, had not the Prime Minister suggested, in order to bolster up his position, that nothing like what had occurred in England had ever occurred in Canada before. Nothing similar had occurred in Canada before, it is true; but I repeat, something far better in the interest of the taxpayers of Canada had been offered and had been put into effect here before. That is enough for that.
Having arrived at the conclusion after my interview with the Prime Minister and certain of his ministers that I could not get anywhere with part (a) of my proposal, and not feeling confident that I could get anywhere with part (b), I made another statement to this house on the 3rd of December, and this is what I said, in addition to what I have already quoted:
So far such committees have not been set up.
That was referring to the committees I had asked for. I went on:
I indicated that I knew there were difficulties, and I would ask the Prime Minister, if he can and will, to tell the house what the attitude of the government is with respect to that.

War Expenditures-Special Committee
That was not indicating a quarrelsome or querulous mood, was it? I went on:
If the difficulties are such as cannot be surmounted, then I have another concrete suggestion which I desire to lay before the house and the country.
Then I made the suggestion which the Prime Minister has read here to-day, the setting-up of a select committee to deal with the question of expenditures on war account. I made that suggestion. I have never sought by word or intimation or anything else to convey the impression that I did not make the suggestion. But I wish to say this in all candour to the house and the country. When I made that suggestion I never realized the implication that such a committee, if set up, could not make any report to the people or to the country. I did not visualize that. I ought to have had brains enough to see it, but I am sometimes stupid and I make no apology for that. When I read that into the records of the house on the 3rd of December, I did not visualize that such a committee, while they could investigate and examine, could not make a report to the country. What would be the good of such a committee, to my mind, without power to report?
Therefore I went back to the Prime Minister and we discussed this matter. I am bound to say for the most part these discussions were carried on in the friendliest manner, with the greatest candour on both sides. I wish to say to the Prime Minister that when I suggested on one occasion-I think it was on the 24th of February; I am not quite certain but I have the date upstairs although not here-the elimination of the word "current'-, he agreed almost immediately. For that I desire to give him credit. He certainly did agree almost immediately, and he agreed of course to the elimination of the words "for civil defence" for the reasons which he has explained at some length. We did not think they would be appropriate in the circumstances here, he having explained that the words referred to certain services that were not germane to the inquiry or to the matters we had in mind, and that they might well be eliminated. We were of one opinion on that.
As a matter of fact, there were only two points at issue between us all the way through.
I raised them after having discussed these matters with my friends on this side of the house, who pointed them out to me.
First, the committee had no power to report on any expenditures.
fMr. R. B. Hanson.]

speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend what is the meaning of the words "with power to examine witnesses and to report from time to time to the house"?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My right hon. friend took almost two and a half hours or two hours to put forward his point of view in this whole thing, and I am not controverting a large part of what he had to say. I think, as a matter of fact, that the factual history he gave, with some slight discrepancies according to my memory, is fairly accurate. There are just a few points on which we differ. Our point of view differs on this, that I do not agree that it would have anything like the effect he says it would have if we had this inquiry wide open and we were able to make a report upon our examination to the house.
The two points at issue were these. The first was that under the terms of reference as I interpret them, while the committee may examine into expenditures, and as the lesolution is now amended, into past expenditures as well as current, into all expenditures, it has no power to report to the house with respect to these matters under examination. But I am as certain of this as of anything that happened in the course of these negotiations, and I am borne out by my colleague to my left, that the Prime Minister, on one occasion at all events, made this a "must" order. We left the meeting with the clear conviction that this committee must meet in camera, and that at no time would the committee's proceedings be public. Most respectfully but as distinctly and firmly as I can say it, I disagree with that point of view; with this limitation however, that if it develops that information is about to be produced which in the judgment and common sense of the committee would bring aid or comfort to the enemy, then of course the proceedings of the committee with respect to that particular topic should be held in camera.
I will add to that a second consideration: where the safety of the state may be involved.
I make those two exceptions: when in the view of the committee the information, if divulged, would be a source of comfort to [Mr. Mackenzie King.l
the enemy, and where the safety of the state may be involved. Those are analogous; they are not coterminous. With those two exceptions I suggest to hon. members that this committee should operate with open doors in order that the public may know what is going on. I warn the Prime Minister that if he refuses to heed this word of advice, if this committee is to meet in camera, the public will be entitled to draw any inferences they wish to draw. The public are suspicious now; why make them more suspicious?
The Prime Minister has already made some concession with respect to one aspect of the matter, and I am going to close my remarks with a plea to him. He says the government has nothing to hide. I have never suggested that there was anything to hide, although I think there is ample evidence of gross extravagance in this war effort. I am bound to say, as I have said here before, that to a certain extent this is inevitable in war time. You just cannot get people to spend money in war time as properly as they would spend it in peace time. There are not the safeguards and the surrounding circumstances in war time that would compel them to be more careful. Then there is the question of haste; time won't wait and things have to be done to-day that cannot possibly be put off until to-morrow, or so they will tell you. Of course usually that is ninety-nine per cent wrong, but it all costs money and there has been great waste.
I close with this plea to the Prime Minister, that if he will not allow this committee to report to the House of Commons on past and current expenditures-and I am not going to fight for that principle any longer-I do suggest to him that he should not let it be said that this committee must meet in secret, save and except for the two considerations I have mentioned.

The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has indicated that the reference to this committee is considerably larger than the corresponding reference to the committee at Westminster. The committee set up in London has been restricted to the investigation of current expenditures, but the word "current" does not appear in the present reference to this committee. I assume that there is an essential difference between the public accounts committee and the special committee

War Expenditures-Special Committee
which is proposed to be set up by this resolution. The public accounts committee is in the nature of a postmortem to determine what has happened and the causes of that happening. This committee has a much wider function to perform. It may look into past expenditures, but the purpose of looking into such expenditures would be to eliminate waste and extravagance in present expenditures.
May I say to the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) who has just spoken, that I would be the last person in this house to say that we in Canada should follow automatically what is done in the British house. I think we all agree with him in that statement. I suggest, however, that the British parliament is an excellent model to follow in the present case. The British House of Commons set up a committee during the first great war to investigate current expenditures with a view to avoiding waste and extravagance. Immediately upon the outbreak of the present war, a similar committee was set up in London.
I think that we in this country might well follow the lead of Great Britain, not only in the present war but in the last war. Both committees, the committee of the great war and the committee of the present war; accomplished excellent results and saved the people of Great Britain, I think it may safely be said, millions of pounds by the close scrutiny which they gave to current expenditures with the object of effecting economies and avoiding extravagance.
I said a moment ago that the model of the British committee was an excellent one to follow, and I am strongly of that opinion in spite of the fact that there may be differences between our system of government and theirs, although such differences are really more on the surface than in reality. The British committee, both in the present war and: in the last one, sat always in camera. It has made, during the present war, fourteen reports to the British House of Commons. It has made a large number of recommendations, some to the government itself and some to individual departments of the government. Most of these recommendations were accepted. Some were not accepted; some were rejected. But the committee made its recommendations after careful inquiry and with a definite purpose to find out the real facts. I submit to every member of this house that a committee sitting in camera can conduct a more thorough and more careful inquiry than can any public accounts committee, where one sees on both sides persons making speeches for the purpose of publicity. If a committee sits in camera, and if the members of that committee are properly seized of their responsibilities, they will be concerned
with ascertaining the real facts and will not be in the least concerned with making speeches or attracting publicity to their utterances.
The British committee resolved itself into several	subcommittees.	Each	subcommitteewas charged with specific and definite responsibilities. The chairmen of these subcommittees, together with the chairman of the committee, constituted a coordinating committee which guided and controlled the several activities of the	subcommittees.	The	subcommitteesworked	collaterally and	at the same time,according to the rules that each laid down for the conduct of its inquiry. The subcommittees listened to witnesses,	visited	plants, visited
public works, visited military sites, conducted such inquiries as they thought were advisable for the purpose of discharging the responsibilities that were cast upon them, and periodically reported their findings back to the general committee, and the committee made its reports from time to time to the house.
The British committee made, I think, a fair and thorough inquiry with regard to all the matters that were brought to its attention. Its investigations of officials were brief and to the point. The members were actuated by the desire to find, out the real facts and were not concerned with publicity for any of the individual members of the committee. If the British committee could perform its functions in the admirable manner in which it has performed them then I resent the suggestion that Canadian members of parliament cannot do likewise. I am convinced that if members of the British house can discharge the very heavy and onerous responsibilities that have been cast upon them, then members of the Canadian House of Commons, whether they are on the government side of the house or the opposition, can equally discharge the equally difficult and onerous responsibilities that are placed upon them, I know that this committee can serve a useful public purpose.
We are asking the Canadian people to give to Canada's war effort all that they can spare out of their savings. I think it is our duty as members of parliament to assure the Canadian people that every possible safeguard is being taken to make certain that every dollar contributed by them shall go as far as possible in our war effort.
I believe that every member of this house is committed to an all-out war effort on the part of Canada. We want the support of every Canadian in this country, and I think we owe it to Canadians throughout Canada that they should be certain, so far as it is within our power as members of parliament to make it so, that every possible economy shall be put into effect and every possible safeguard taken against extravagance in expenditures.

That, I believe, can be done by a thorough and careful inquiry without regard to publicity. We will not be concerned in the committee as to what the public thinks; we will be concerned with the knowledge within ourselves, as members of the committee, that we are doing an honest and thorough job of investigation. That will be the important thing, and I think that in that regard the committee might well enlist the support of eyerv member of the house. The British committee did that. The British committee addressed a circular letter to every member of the House of Commons asking the members to indicate the lines of inquiry which they thought the committee should follow and the various matters which, in the opinion of the members, should be brought to the attention of the committee. That might be done.
Then, too, I have no doubt that when the committee is set up, suggestions of one kind and another, from one end of Canada to the other, will come to the committee, and these suggestions will be explored and investigated. They will be sorted out and sent to this or that subcommittee for careful investigation and exploration, and I think, if we as members of the House of Commons approach this very difficult and onerous task with a full appreciation of the great responsibility that is cast upon us, we shall be performing a truly national and patriotic service. Every member of this house who is named on this committee is a Canadian, concerned with the Canadian war effort and with its success, and I believe I may safely pledge in their name every member of this committee to an honest, fair and impartial inquiry into all the matters that are referred to the committee.
The committee has power to make reports from time to time to the house. It is not circumscribed in its other activities. It may Irom time to time report informally to the head of the department concerned or to the Prime Minister with a view to bringing about economies, with a view to eliminating waste, with a view to the avoidance of extravagance. Not the least useful function of this committee will be its very existence and the knowledge on the part of the spending authorities in the state that this committee is in existence and will be supervising and considering and inquiring into their expenditures. That alone will be worth the establishment of the committee.
There is nothing in the present resolution as to the powers of the committee to adjourn from place to place, nor is there anything in the resolution to empower the committee to sit during a recess of the house, nor is there anything to empower subcommittees of the general committee to have the powers of the
[Mr. Thorson.J
general committee, but all of these matters can be dealt with as the necessity for them arises.
I will close with this remark, Mr. Speaker, that if we approach this committee with the same attitude of mind that actuated the British committee, I see no reason why we should not serve a very useful purpose; and if members of the British House of Commons can discharge their responsibilities in a manner becoming to the best traditions of the British house, I see no reason why members of the Canadian House of Commons should not do likewise.

committee will do a great work for Canada and will greatly strengthen the war effort of our nation.
Here we are facing the fight of our history, with young Canadians by the thousand exposed to sudden death this very night, with thousands of wives and mothers at home wondering what to-morrow may bring for their loved ones, with thousands of children in Canada wondering what is going to happen to their daddy. Surely at such a time this house can forget politics on this one question and the members of this committee can go into its meetings with their minds made up that they will do their very best not only to cut down expenditures and find where money is being wasted but also to suggest ways in which our war effort can be improved. That, as the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) has so well said, has been the result in the British House of Commons. I know the private members of this house well enough to know that the same thing can be done here.
As I have said before, I hold that the private members are the back-bone of this parliament. They are the men who really count in this house, with all due deference to the ministers. This is the chance for the private members of this House of Commons to show what they are made of. I am certain that they will do that job and do it well. I am named on the committee and, like the others, I intend to do my part to the very best of my ability and as a Canadian first, last and all the time. I would ask the hon. members not on the committee to be behind us in this effort; give us a chance to prove to the Canadian people that the Canadian parliament can really get results without becoming involved in partisan political quarrels.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE
APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The
war was only a few days old when I asked for the appointment of a similar committee to the one set out in the text of this resolution, and to consider Canada's war effort in general. In my opinion the resolution does not go far enough; it is just a postmortem and an inquest and a grand assize held into only one feature of the war effort that is gone and gone forever beyond recall, namely, Canada being too late all along the line.
The text of the resolution does not provide for what the people of this country are demanding. I do not speak in a partisan sense, far from it, because I know no politics in this house except the effective conduct of the war. Those who want to conduct politics can do so, but in the last war and in this war I know no politics.
For over one hundred years there was civil war in England to get control of expenditures. The House of Commons here, since this war started, has been the forgotten agency in our constitutional system of government. We in this house have been the forgotten men; the private member has no rights; he can object to nothing, because these expenditures are made under the War Measures Act. Many outside boards have been created which were never in existence in the great war, with authority over the head body, the House of Commons of Canada; we never had them when we had our five allies. We have no control over the expenditure or over what is being done.
The text of the resolution does not go far enough. It is just a resolution to appoint a committee. The public accounts committee has always acted, in matters like this, in all the wars in England and the dominions, but here the public accounts committee has never been asked to sit. The money has been spent and we have an auditor general. It is spent for defence services; but what are defence services; what are foreign services; what are external services? No one knows.

subtopic: SEVERANCE OF DIPLOMATIC RELATIONS WITH BULGARIA AND ROUMANIA-PROSCRIBED TERRITORIES

speechtext:
.Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):	Mr. Speaker, I should
like to make a brief statement to the house on the present situation in the Balkans, as it affects nationals and citizens of certain of those countries.
Acting upon instructions from the government of the United Kingdom, His Majesty's minister at Sofia has broken off diplomatic relations with Bulgaria to-day. There is no Canadian diplomatic mission in Bulgaria and there are no Bulgarian diplomatic or consular representatives in this country. There was, therefore, no occasion for any action by the Canadian government with regard to the severance of diplomatic relations.
The breaking off of diplomatic relations does pot necessarily bring about a state of war. On the other hand, in breaking off diplomatic relations the United Kingdom felt it could not overlook the action of the Bulgarian government in aligning Bulgaria with the axis powers and in permitting German forces to enter Bulgaria and to use that country as a base from which to conduct hostile operations.
Action has been taken and is being taken by the Canadian government to protect Canadian interests during the period that may intervene between the breaking off of diplomatic relations and actual hostilities should such take place. Action has already been taken by order in council making Bulgaria proscribed territory which means that all transactions with Bulgaria will be subjected to the regime of the trading with the enemy regulations. In this manner it is made unlawful to
conduct any transactions involving, directly or indirectly, economic aid to the enemy. Precautionary action is being undertaken to prevent any transactions that might result in assistance to the enemy.
Police action that is necessary to preserve the security of the state is, of course, being undertaken. While this is so, Bulgarian nationals and persons of Bulgarian descent will not be disturbed so long a§ they show by their conduct that they are rendering loyal obedience to the law's and institutions of this country.
The action taken to make Bulgaria proscribed territory extends also to Hungary. Hungary is a country w'ith which diplomatic relations are maintained by the United Kingdom. On the other hand it is not possible entirely to overlook the fact that Hungary is contiguous to territory under German domination, and Hungary's alignment with the axis and the according by Hungary to the enemy of privileges which are not consistent with neutrality. Hungary maintains a consulate general in Montreal and a consulate in Winnipeg. The action taken in making Hungary-proscribed territory has subjected transactions with that country to the regime of the trading with the enemy regulations and makes it possible to prevent transactions that might be of advantage to the enemy. The measures taken are precautionary and consistent with the continuation of existing regulations. [DOT]
Diplomatic relations between the United Kingdom and Roumania were broken off on the 10th of February of this year. Subsequently the consul general of Roumania in Canada received instructions from his government to close the consulate general in Montreal, and this action was taken on the 15th February of this year. The consul general and his staff have withdrawn. Roumania was made proscribed territory and other precautionary measures were undertaken similar to those which are being adopted with regard to Bulgaria. In the case of Roumanian nationals, and persons of Roumanian descent, the same position is maintained as in the case of Bulgarians. They will not be disturbed so long as their conduct conforms to our laws, and is consistent with the allegiance which, under the laws of Canada, is due from all residents, irrespective of their national status or racial origin.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: INTERPRETATION OF STANDING ORDER 41 RESPECTING THE TABLING OF LETTERS QUOTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would ask if your honour would kindly take into consideration standing order 41 and give an interpretation particularly of paragraphs 315 and 316 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms which have a bearing on the tabling of letters. We have had a discussion of this point on previous occasions in the house but I cannot find any definite ruling. I cite paragraph 316 under standing order 41:
It has been admitted that a document which has been cited ought to be laid upon the table of the house, if it can be done without injury to the public interest. The same rule, however, cannot be held to apply to private letters or memoranda. .
The preceding paragraph puts another limitation upon the same matter. Paragraph 315 says:
A minister of the crown is not at liberty to read or quote from a dispatch or other state paper not before the house, unless he be prepared to lay it upon the table.
It goes on to say:
This restraint is similar to the rule of evidence in courts of law, which prevent counsel from citing documents which have not been produced in evidence. The principle is so

Rules of the House
reasonable that it has not been contested; and when the objection has been made in time, it has been generally acquiesced in.
And now I read the last part of paragraph 316:
On the 18th May, 1865, the attorney general, on being asked by Mr. Ferrard if he would lay upon the table a written statement and a letter to which he had referred on a previous day, in assuming a question relative to the Leeds bankruptcy court, replied that he had made a statement to the house upon his own responsibility, and that the documents he had referred to being private, he could not lay them upon the table. Lord Robert Cecil contended that the papers, having been cited, should be produced; but the Speaker declared that this rule applied to public documents only.
If we could get a ruling on this point, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be helpful.

maintopic: INTERPRETATION OF STANDING ORDER 41 RESPECTING THE TABLING OF LETTERS QUOTED

have to giving a ruling is that there is nothing before the chair and the Speaker is really not called upon to give advice to 'hon. members unless the question is brought up in the course of discussion or debate. At the moment I am not in a position to give a ruling, but if the question arises in the course of debate or some proceeding of the house, then of course I would be prepared to give a ruling.

speechtext:
I wish to bring up a,
matter which was referred to the other day by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson). I protest against the charges that are aimed at the business men of Toronto and, for that matter, business men throughout the country. I do not believe for a moment that the business men of Canada are "resting on their oars." Those in Toronto are working night and d>ay to speed up Canada's war effort, some of them losing money. Some are not able to get parts, and others are waiting for extensions of plants. If there is any district that is making its contribution in men and munitions, it is military district No. 2. What I say of the business men of Toronto is true, I -have no doubt, of the industrialists of the country generally.
Some reference has been made to farmers'1 sons. I am glad to hear the minister's assurance that the committee can deal with these-matters. I am sure he never has anything to hide in his hard work. Let me assure the house that the sons of farmers in Ontario are-not asking to be exempted. May I say to the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Gardiner) that had it not been for him and his useless department, we should have had
800,000	soldiers trained by now on the voluntary system of recruiting instead of the cumbersome machinery of the mobilization department.
Yesterday the funeral of a great Canadian, Sir Frederick Banting, was held in Toronto. He was born on the farm, but look what he, a patriot in peace and war alike, did for his country. Speaking in this house on May 16, 1923. I mentioned the patriotism of the farmers of Ontario when the issue of protection was raised. The farmers of Ontario have never failed to stand for their country in the polling booths; and when war has threatened the existence of this dominion, the farmers of Ontario-the actual farmers- have never failed to go themselves or to send their sons to defend their country on the battlefield.
This resolution speaks for itself. I do not see why hon. gentlemen in another place, as they are called, should not have their services utilized in this war effort. The senate at Washington and the House of Lords in England are not, like ours, on holidays. The government might very well give the other chamber more work to do, coordinated and cooperated with the work of this house, particularly in this time of war, because they have some very valuable business men and war leaders there. How will Britain be able to take the offensive unless the dominions do their duty with regard to men and munitions?
1262	COMMONS
War Expenditures-Special Committee
This committee should have the power also to go over the expenditures of the joint defence board which has been set up. That board proposes to spend a large amount of money, and we do not know what it is all about. Not long ago we had an announcement made by the deputy minister of the naval department, the minister himself, and officials of the joint defence board, involving an expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars, without this House of Commons knowing anything about the matter.
What about our arms programme, which is still in the preparatoiy stage? Will the work of this committee hinder or help our war effort? Is the committee to act on party lines, or is it not? Should the party principle not be eliminated? Many young soldiers who have enlisted to fight Hitler would not have done so voluntarily if they had known they were going to be sent to the West Indies, or Iceland, or Greenland's icy mountains. Hitler cannot be fought there; those are secondary areas. In our whole war effort we seem to be ignoring the danger to Great Britain, particularly in the Mediterranean, where England is doing so well against the Italians. If Britain loses the war, however, the Germans will make these same Italians fight against Britain, and Britain has to feed them and take good care of them.
If this committee is simply to conduct a postmortem on what has been done in the past, it had better not be appointed. It should have power to go over and review the work of outside boards as well. Many men in Canada have been lulled into a false sense of security. They might have known that unless those countries desiring peace were stronger than those desiring war, there would he no peace. I define collective security as a doctrine that leaves to others the task of defending freedom and civilization on land, sea and in the air, while they look on as spectators.
In conclusion, I fail to see how the appointment of this committee will help. We do not want a whitewash repetition of what was done once before in another committee on railways and shipping; we want to get some real action. The press has a right, as I see it, to carry on free discussion and criticism. The press has an important duty to perform. All the information given out through the government information bureau might just as well be dropped. It has been a cardinal principle of the nazi regime, and one of its proudest accomplishments, to take away the freedom of the press. In Canada I think the press are measuring up to their duty splendidly, particularly in connection with the war loans
{Mr. Church.]
campaign. If the press is to fulfil these functions adequately, there must be a large number of independent newspapers, each representing a particular viewpoint. The national press should provide a medium for the expression of opinion. A democratic press reflects public opinion, and the right of free discussion should not be taken away. In a double sense the press is an intermediary between the government and the public. It provides a channel by which ministers can keep the electorate informed of their activities, and it also serves as a sort of barometer, by means of which the government can gauge the feelings of the country. These are the views of a great newspaper man, and patriot, Mr. Arthur Mann, the brilliant editor of the Yorkshire Post. He says:
In this connection the establishment of the ministry of information by the present government betrayed, in its original form, a lack of confidence in the ability of the press to fulfil its proper functions.
I believe that something should be done now to establish the freedom of the press and to protect it for the period of the war. This committee may meet until doomsday, but unless it is given proper powers and functions, I do not believe any good will flow from it, and the people will continue to be just as much in the dark with regard to Canada's war effort.

I do not think the Prime Minister is taking any chances on the deliberations of the committee being used for political advantage. Some question has been raised as to whether the deliberations should be held in camera. At the moment I believe that most of these meetings could be thrown wide open to the public. As a member of one of the minority groups I wish to register a protest with respect to the conferences which were held between the Prime Minister and some members of his party and certain members of the official opposition regarding this question. It does seem to me that representation from the minority groups should have been invited. It would have been a fine gesture on the part of the Prime Minister to issue such an invitation. The Prime Minister will find that the members of the minority groups are just as much interested in these important matters as are the members of either of the majority groups. The Prime Minister in my opinion missed an excellent opportunity to practise that virtue of cooperation which he professes to admire.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to delay the passage of this resolution, but being one of the few new members of the house selected to serve on this committee, and one of the thirteen Liberal lawyers to whom the hon. member who has just taken his seat referred, there are a few matters which I think I should bring to the attention of the house.
When the committee was first proposed in November or December last, I was delighted at the suggestion. I was not too much concerned about who should get the credit; I felt that it was a constructive move which would enable private members of this house to render real public service. I have heard it said that the activities of private members were limited, that their hands, particularly those of the large government majority, were more or less tied. That suggestion has been put forth by some of my hon. friends opposite. Let me say at once that I have not found that to be so. So far as this committee is concerned, if I find, as someone has suggested, that I am to act as part of a whitewashing operation, I shall ask to be relieved of my duties on the committee.
I cannot for the life of me see why the work of this committee should be looked at from a partisan point of view. It seems to me that its work can be carried on in a perfectly non-partisan way. I was delighted to hear the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) say last evening in no uncertain terms that he hoped that when the members went into the first meeting of the committee and every subsequent meeting they would leave their politics behind. Unfortunately that view does not seem to be held by all, and certainly not by certain sections of the press. The debate which occurred last evening did not entirely convince me that it was shared by all hon. gentlemen opposite.
I do not propose to enter into a discussion as to whether the meetings of this committee should be secret or open. Personally I can think of many reasons why the meetings should be held in camera. I can see no good reason for holding them in public, unless it is to afford an opportunity to some one to display his ability, or lack of

IFar Expenditures-Special Committee
it, as a cross-examiner. I cannot help feeling that behind the criticism which has been voiced in the press, and to a certain extent by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), there is a belief that the representation of the Liberal party on this committee is too large. Personally I resent the implication, if implication there be, that because I sit on that committee as a Liberal member I am not going to do my duty.
May I be allowed to make a personal reference? I was elected in the last election as a Liberal, but I believe it is fair to say that I received possibly as many Conservative votes as some of the hon. gentlemen opposite. My opponent was a gentleman who had sat in this house for many years. I think I can say without fear of contradiction that he had the respect, admiration and affection, not only of the members of the house but of his constituents. I refer, of course, to Mr. R. S. White. Mr. White was elected in 1935 with a large majority, something over 5,500. I was elected last year with a slightly larger majority. I am not under the delusion that that was due to any special ability on my part; it was due to the fact that the electors preferred the policies offered by the present government to those put forward by Doctor Manion. I like to think that the size of my majority was due in some measure to the confidence which a large number of the electors, both Conservative and Liberal, had in myself. I like to think that they felt that if I came here I would do what I could to ensure that our war effort would be the maximum of which we are capable. For that reason I have been particularly disturbed at the suggestion that was made-I do not say that the suggestion was made with respect to myself- that Liberal members as such will not act on this committee in a non-partisan way. I feel that criticism of that sort, if sincere, is going to produce exactly the opposite effect from that intended.
I know there is a good deal of nonsense talked about criticism. Criticism, of course, is an absolutely necessary part of our democratic system. It cannot function without it. I am not very much concerned about all this talk of the distinction between constructive and destructive criticism. To me it is too hard to tell what the difference is. What I am more interested in is whether the critic is sincere and what the motive is which actuates him in putting forward his criticism. I cannot help feeling that a great deal of the criticism which has been put forward in the press and in this house as to the way in which this committee will function, while 14873-81
perhaps sincere, is not motivated solely, if at all, by a desire to see that a thorough and proper investigation be made into our war expenditures.
The other day I read the report of a speech which was made in Toronto by the mayor of Hamilton in connection with this question of criticism. It is reported in the Hamilton Spectator of the 27th of February, Thursday last, and I should like to read one or two extracts from that speech:
Mayor W. A. Morrison, K.C., of Hamilton, speaking as a "known Conservative" told the Ontario Good Roads Association in an address to-day that "we must cast out suspicion and carping and bitter criticism" to build up confidence in Canada's government, her public men and war effort.
"The man who destroys confidence in Canada and its leaders to-day is playing the game Germany has often played in other countries of undermining confidence in administrations."
"Rumour is a terrible weapon in the hands of one's enemies-rumour stealthily sown and cultivated by enemy agents has preceded the collapse of every country that has come under the German yoke. Let us be on our guard in these critical times against rumour and the wise guys who keep sniping at Canada's war effort with criticisms and comments based on rumours which have little solid foundation in fact."
Continuing, he said:
Nobody can accuse me of ever having pulled my punches when I have had to mix it in peacetime politics with the Liberals either at Queen's park or at Ottawa, but let me tell you this, when this country is at war I am a Canadian and a Britisher before I am a Conservative party man and, like a lot of other people, I am getting damned well fed up with this constant yapping at the government about the inefficiency and ineffectiveness of the war effort.
I do not know his worship the mayor. He perhaps did not couch his language exactly in parliamentary terms, but he was speaking straight to the point, and I think he was expressing views which are shared by a good many people in this country including, I may say, myself.
I, in common with a good many other members of this house, served overseas in the last war. It is just twenty-four years ago this month that I landed in France as a private soldier in a battery of which the second in command was my hon. friend the member for Queens (Mr. Macmillan).
I was thinking yesterday as I heard my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) referring to these category "Cl" fellows who can walk five miles with a pack on their back, that perhaps I could not even qualify for that to-day. But when I was elected as a member of this house less than a year ago, I felt that in this particular field I might be able to make some contribution to

1266	COMMONS
War Expenditures-Special Committee
the prosecution of this war and I hope to do so. I did feel when this committee was suggested and my name appeared as a member of it that it would accord an opportunity of doing a really constructive job. Frankly, it has been a little discouraging to me to have the discussion of the formation of this committee, both in the press and to a certain extent in this house, put on a partisan basis. Therefore I want to endorse with all the sincerity at my command the views which were so ably expressed last night by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), and to suggest that we get this resolution through so that the committee can get down to work just as soon as possible.

speechtext:
I think, Mr. Speaker, that we are all seized with the great responsibility we have during these difficult times, and I believe that members on all sides will address themselves to any task that is given us, with energy, zeal and industry, with the single purpose of trying to do something on behalf of Canada and the empire. The situation abroad is to-day perhaps even more serious than at any other time. We are seeing an attack upon our ideals and our way of life, only the remnants of which are left in some countries of Europe, and it is not difficult for us to echo the sentiments which the hon. member for St. Antoine-West-mount (Mr. Abbott) expressed a moment or two ago and which were so admirably expressed last night by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green).
Before addressing myself to the question before the chair I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether we are quite in order in this discussion. Would it not have been sufficient for the purposes of this resolution if the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had simply made his statement, followed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), and then perhaps let it go at that? I felt disposed to rise to a point of order when the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) rose in his place, but I suppose he wanted to help out in laying the groundwork for the committee over which he may have the honour to preside.
Frankly, I was disappointed with the statement of the Prime Minister as to the functions of this committee. The evidence his statement gave of faltering, of not being just sure of what the committee might be able to do, not laying down the principles which should govern the committee, leaving the impression which he did last December that the committee would proceed on much the same lines as the committee at Westminster, neglecting to act last December on this

tremendous job of work, of which now we can touch only the fringe, and allowing that work to lie untouched from then until now- all this showed a definite weakness.
Among the names of members whom it is proposed to appoint to this committee, I have the honour to notice my own. I did not ask to be placed on this committee. Without any suggestion from myself, I was asked to serve on it, and I assume that responsibility, realizing that I shall have a free hand and that the sole purpose of our deliberations shall be the helping of our war effort. Many of our forefathers are buried overseas; our children are willing to spill their blood in the cause, and many of them are already over there. From the point of view of the people themselves, we must exert durselves to do everything we possibly can.
Then, on the material side, be it noted that our industries are connected and closely allied with British empire industries. The possibilities of our earning a living in the days to come are tied up with our membership in the empire. No matter from what point of view we look at the problem, we are forced to the conclusion that this must be an all-out effort.
To my mind this effort, since the inception of the war, and even before it, has been narrowed and circumscribed through the attitude of the government that it is their responsibility and theirs alone. Press and public rise indignantly to assert that the government must broaden the effort. So it chooses executives from industry, from the schools of learning and from institutions of (public service, and appoints them to assist in this and that way. That is all to the good, and I am thoroughly in accord with it. But when restrictions are placed upon those who come to serve, when they find themselves circumscribed and inhibited by political necessities, it is difficult for them to function. We are now to have a committee which is to lay all party and partisan considerations on the doormat before it enters upon its deliberations. That is a fine objective, and if I am honoured with a place upon the committee, everything in my power will be done to try to reach that objective. But all we have to go on is the experience of days gone by. I address myself particularly now to those who will be privileged to serve on that committee, and since some of them have not been here during the whole of the last two decades, we will restrict our observations and merely look fairly in the face what has occurred in the last ten months with regard to committees which have been reviewing expenditures.
What do we find? The one example which stands out above all others, of a committee

War Expenditures-Special Committee
anxious to do work on behalf of Canada, is the one which reviewed the accounts of the railways. The close of the calendar year coincides with the closing of the books of the Canadian National Railways. A committee was set up to examine into expenditures and the budget for the coming year. I believe that its report was tabled, in February a year ago, and in that report a vote of $15 million was asked in connection w'ith the budget for the coming year. Then we had an election. The report was not considered. The months of March and April went by, and in May parliament reassembled. In the meantime, expanding revenues on all our railway lines, the result of increased car loadings week by week and other items of that kind, pointed to the fact that $15 million would not be needed. When the committee reconvened, this was brought to its attention. I challenge any member of that committee to assert that that money was needed. They knew in their hearts, when they were sitting last June, and it was brought to their attention that that sum would not be required, that there was no necessity, in view of the experience of the months which had intervened, for any such sum. Yet the committee examining expenditure and budgeting for future expenditure drew a party line when the vote was taken and, to a man, the partisan group, led by a minister of the crown, voted to provide $15 million in case they might want to spend it.
I say to those who may serve on the present committee, let us have no approach of that kind to the problem which now faces us. I here and now give notice that any such approach will find me, if I am honoured with an appointment, withdrawing from the committee.
Here is another example of the like kind. Two-thirds of the revenue of the Trans-Canada Air Lines comes from the Post Office Department. Its rates, and of course necessarily so, are far in excess of what obtain on air lines in other countries, but the excess has enabled them to finish their business for the year with a substantial surplus. AH sensible men know that, in starting projects of this kind, one does not look for substantial surpluses, and if they occur, it is natural to examine whence they come. In this case they came out of one department and went into the other. I do not complain so much about that, provided the fact is admitted.
Coming to the partisan side of that picture, what do we find? We find in the report a statement to the effect that they had earned their interest charges, they had earned their depreciation charges and showed this surplus.

The real fact of the matter was-and the members of that committee knew it-that these' were bookkeeping figures, that sixty cents per flight mile was paid for the carriage of mail, whether mail was carried or not, when the service was worth no more than nineteen or twenty cents. The money which made that showing possible came by reason of a contract which was not sound and, as regards the-amount of money used to subsidize that project, would not bear investigation. Yet members of that committee rose in their places and voted to a man on party lines to endorse a statement in the report which was not borne out when the examination was made.
We can go back to other days. I do not use the word "whitewash" which was employed by my hon. friend (Mr. Church) a few minutes ago. It describes rather well, however, what happened in the days of the customs investigation, what happened in the price spreads investigation, yes, and what has happened in every committee that has sat on any special problem in the last twenty years to my own knowledge.
I do not feel disposed to prejudge a case which we might be asked to sit on. I am surprised that the hon. member for Selkirk, a learned gentleman, should rise in his place and try to indicate what is going to happen when the committee convenes. I will therefore reserve any remarks with regard to the conduct of the committee except to say that I am in accord with what my hon. leader had to say. I was in accord with his original idea that there should be perhaps two committees or two sections of this committee, namely
(a)	a section having to do with the men themselves, our soldiers, sailors and airmen, and
(b)	a section having to do with the material side. I rather concur in his admitting the view expressed by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) and I will let it go at that.
In the view expressed by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) I concur. I do not see how we can go into a committee that sits in camera on a project of this magnitude. It is quite true they sat in camera at Westminster and brought down some fourteen reports. The Prime Minister knows and this house knows that many of the deliberations, or parts of the deliberations, of these secret subcommittees found their way into the press of the country from time to time. Hon. members well know that if such a committee sitting in camera convenes in this House of Commons, leaks will get into the press. Did we not have an example of that within the last two or three days? The Prime Minister occupied most of his time in finding fault

War Expenditures-Special Committee
with what had leaked out from a very small group, much smaller and much more subject to questioning than the one proposed to be set up. But men charged with this responsibility are not going to give out facts or figures, or quantities or information that will be of any comfort to the enemy. If we do, we are not worthy to sit on the committee. If members of this house do such a thing, they are not worthy to sit in the house. We are studying the problem with a view to assisting in every way possible.
A great deal of time is wasted in discussing the word "current." We know what the word "current" means, and we know that the impression has prevailed in the country since the house adjourned in December that the inquiry was only going to be from this time forward, instead of going back to what had happened before. But it will be very difficult to examine even current expenditures. We do not know what they are and we are not getting statements which are frank enough. We are not getting statements which are sufficiently up to the minute to give us an opportunity to examine even into current expenditures.
On several occasions during the last two sessions I had the privilege of rising in my place and asking the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) to lay on the table contracts awarded months previously. Just yesterday the minister laid on the table contracts awarded for the month of November, 1940. Are we to be able to examine anything that has happened since November? Of course we must be able to. After all, this department only requires clerical help and management to bring the information up to date. Some business institutions close their books on Thursday and a statement of their affairs is on the desk for Saturday. That *obtains in four or five industries in which I am interested. They are small-a matter of a couple of hundred men-but it can be done. Business houses mailed their statements of accounts for the month of March last Friday evening at five o'clock, that being the last day of the month previous, and they were in the hands of their customers on Saturday morning, March 1. It is being done. One of the largest institutions in Canada closes its books at five o'clock on Friday night and on Saturday morning there is the financial statement for the week's business on the desk of every executive. I know that to be a fact. I say, it can be done, and in this case it must be done, so that we shall have an opportunity to be up to the moment.
I mentioned the word "frankness" and I will *mention it again. Perhaps it is not a lack of frankness so much as a lack of attention, on <
the part of the organizations in our government which are spending money, to what is being said in the House of Commons. Perhaps some civil servants do not realize that this parliament is supreme. Perhaps, from some of the discussions that go on here, they come to the conclusion that we do not know what it is all about, and they have no intention of letting us know. I do not know. At any rate, I would refer to two returns which came down in the last couple of days, one of them with regard to the purchase of lands in the township of Scarboro for the building of some munitions enterprise or other, involving a matter of some three or four hundred acres. The return comes down, "No information". The contractors are building on that land now. The land was expropriated and taken over months ago. In like manner a return was brought down, which I asked for in my own name, with regard to the township of Pickering-"No information". They entered on these lands in October last and tore down fences and buildings. I made the inquiry for the reason that certain persons wanted to see whether they could help on that job. Trucks are out there to-day clearing off the buildings and getting ready for a considerable expenditure, which I notice runs into as much as 82,000,000, one-eighth for Canadian account and seven-eighths for United Kingdom account. Yet the return comes to the house, "No information".
