The hon. member for Selkirk, in discussing the appointment of this committee, made the suggestion that when we oppose the idea of its being a secret committee, we are just scratching the surface of the matter and not getting down to realities. I suppose the group who will surround him in that committee will follow through on his suggestion that, in part at least, it must be held in camera. When the hon. member took that attitude he was following the lead that was given by the Prime Minister, but yesterday the Prime Minister removed that restriction. I ask now that all members of the government do likewise. There is still on Hansard a statement by the Minister of Munitions and Supply that this committee will sit in camera. Before the debate concludes, I should like the Prime Minister to say that when he withdrew that restriction he did so on behalf of all the members of his cabinet; otherwise I do not see how I can serve on such a committee. I will not serve on a committee that is sitting in camera.
We are faced with a very difficult problem. The magnitude of these expenditures is such that we may be able to touch only the fringe of the job of work ahead of us. Matters will have to be taken up largely on general lines. I hope we shall approach the problem remembering that our country and our empire are facing a ruthless, almost furious enemy, ambitious for power; fanatics who have come to power by crushing and impoverishing: smaller nations, with the backing of a youthful mob who seem to be seized with the idea that the old order of things is not good enough, who wish to establish a new civilization and destroy the old. We British people, slow to anger, have built up over the last thousand years a civilization held together not by force but by unwritten laws and codes of ethics. We have been a great agency for good during that time, and we should continue to be a force for good. That should be the star at which members of this committee should look all the time. They should not be circumscribed by partisanship-and I couple the name of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) with the circumscribing of our effort-and should see if it is not possible for government members of a committee not to be leopards but to change their spots for once. (Translation) This resolution is timely: Its very introduction will prevent many abuses. Therefore, I wish to bring to the attention of the house some facts that are quite unusual, to say the least. We find that the dominion agrees to hand money to industrialists for the manufacture of munitions. In the fulfilment of most contracts, the expense is borne by the Canadian government, except perhaps, for a contribution from the United Kingdom. These contracts are awarded to this or that firm, very often without public tenders having first been called. In many cases, the firm which secures the contract does not fulfil it itself, but entrusts the work to sub-contractors. Why should there be any middlemen? Whenever a third party comes in, the expenditure invariably increases, costly transactions take place, with all that is entailed by the transfer of negotiable instruments that are part of the contracts from a legal standpoint. Yet we have in Canada a large number of industries able to offer the dominion every necessary /guarantee in addition to assuming themselves df not all at least a substantial part of the .advances. Moreover, the financial position [DOT]of this country, as well as the public interest, -would be better protected if the tender system once again was resorted to in the award of all contracts. Besides, would not such a procedure best ensure fairness and honesty? It is important that the government should eliminate middlemen by entrusting the direct fulfilment of contracts to well-established firms, whose responsibility and solvency could hot be questioned. The committee provided for in this resolution should seriously examine the matter and give special consideration to what I am about to say.
At this time, I am keeping in mind the urgent necessity for the government to hound down everywhere those who contrive to reap a harvest through patronage, through an odious exploitation of munition factory workers whereby the latter are sneakily deprived of wages sufficient for the support of their dependents with the result that they receive little in return for their work. The government must by every means at their command destroy those despicable and vile scoundrels, as they must also remove shameless financiers and histrionic politicians from the scene where not only our future but our very existence is now at stake. At this time when we are required to make very heavy sacrifices, let war be waged upon combine-advocating politicians, responsible for almost all the abuses that exist to-day. Party lobbyists should not be allowed to gain the upper 
hand in this country, whose debt is piling up from day to day. Public interest, nay the very safety of our nation makes it a duty for true statesmen, for political men worthy of that name, to restrain that swarming mob which may jeopardize the success of the most commendable policies. Men engaged in that racket, in that organized, or I should rather say industrialized crime, since it is taking nowadays alarming proportions, are endeavouring to operate, through the hiring of workmen, even in munition plants. Have we not seen an aftermath of their activities in proceedings taken before courts of justice in Montreal? The people who pay have a right to demand every necessary precaution against the plots of those people who are truly sabotaging the defence and the war effort of Canada.
Let us forestall the baneful intrigues of robbers who are so unconcerned about the people's welfare that they have repeatedly betrayed the nation for the furtherance of their petty interests. As a means of rooting out the evil, I would suggest to the right honourable the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) to have all armament factories in Canada watched by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Nobody would have any complaint to make on that score. It would be in the mutual interests of industrialists and workmen, and greedy foremen would find it impossible to exploit wage earners.
A short time ago, the public information office released to editors of religious news an article entitled "By Whom is Right Upheld," which I wish to quote:
One merely has to compare the nazi traditions and war aims with those of England and her allies to ascertain who is upholding right in this conflict wherein the fate of the world is at stake. Let us recall a statement of principles, similar to the one made by His Holiness the Pope, which has recently been published by English churchmen, one of whom was His Eminence Cardinal Hinsley. archbishop of Westminster and Roman Catholic primate of England. They made five suggestions:
Excessive inequality in wealth should be abolished.
Every child, of whatever race or condition, should have an equal opportunity to secure an education commensurate with his talents and needs.
The family must be maintained as a social unit.
The sense of a divine mission must again inspire man in his daily work.
The world's resources must be used as a gift imparted by God to all men, according to the needs of the present and future generations.
Is that not a complete program of social regeneration? One of the war aims of the allies is the defence and preservation of democracy. Of course, all forms of govern-

War Expenditures-Special Committee
ment are handicapped by imperfections inherent in their contingent and human nature. For that very reason should they not ever strive after justice, honesty, and sound and true freedom, which cannot possibly be derived from the favouritism and ambition of exploiters, who invariably subordinate the welfare of the people to their own interests? Those who shed and will shed their blood in upholding the principles stated in the war aims of the allies have a right to demand that their sacrifice shall not have been made in vain. All those whom the nation is mobilizing in their persons, their life, their industry, their home, their work, their income, demand that necessary action be taken against traitors, saboteurs, monopolizers and supporters of financial imperialism. The first duty of the government is to afford such protection to the utmost of their unlimited powers.

Mr. Speaker, with regard to this committee I should like to express an opinion which, up to the present time, I believe has not been brought to the attention of the house. I am not going to say whether I would or would not serve on a committee which sat in camera, or otherwise. In my opinion that would be a wrong basis on which to start. When one goes into a committee he should try to do the things the majority believe to be in the best interests of all. Therefore I would not say I would not serve on a committee if it chose to do thus or so.
I believe the committee may do a great deal of good. In the first place it will serve as a warning to those who would prosper on the misfortunes of others, or those who would not conduct their affairs on an ethical basis. Second, in addition to the good effect it will have on the people, and the impression it will leave in the minds of those people that the interests of the taxpayers are being looked after, there is another feature to which I believe consideration must be given. In thinking of it we must first say to ourselves: What is the job we have in hand at the present [DOT]time? Is it the job of retarding the war effort, or that of promoting the war effort?
I now ask the house to consider for a moment whether a committee of this kind will actually promote, facilitate or speed up the present war effort. That in my opinion is paramount. What is going to be the effect on those people who are constantly having to make decisions with regard to war contracts, the purchase of lands, the types of aeroplanes or boats to be built, if they think that every move they make is going to be brought before a committee of the house for examination?
In peace time I believe every move they make should be watched. But in a time like this, when speed is necessary, I would question the wisdom of the appointment of a committee which would make such examinations. If it is appointed, then I say the committee must be very careful that by methods of obstruction it does not add to the cost of the war effort more than the few dollars or even the few thousands of dollars it might save. If criticism of this house is justified, more than anything else it is because we have failed to get quick decisions on a number of matters. I am not condemning the war effort or the work of this government, but I do say that decisions are vital in the interests of this country. I doubt if we shall be able to get decisions quickly if those who are to make them have to wait to wrap up everything in a blue parcel, tie it with red ribbon and put a seal upon it.
Mr. DOUGLAS G. ROSS (St. Paul's): Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to delay the passage of this resolution or to speak at great length, but there are one or two observations I should like to make. I agree with what was said by my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), when he suggested that the House of Commons should give its blessing to this committee so that it could get on with its work. I feel also that the success of this committee depends upon the extent to which the members of the committee are willing to leave their politics outside the door of the committee room. The members of that committee will have practically to forsake their politics for the duration of the war, both in and out of this house. Anything I may say to-day I do not want to be taken as casting reflection upon any hon. member. It is of the utmost importance that this committee should work in the greatest harmony possible, and there should be similar harmony in connection with the setting up of the committee. Yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made a few remarks which I do not think were altogether fair. He quoted an editorial which had appeared in the Globe and Mail, as follows:
It is not to be expected that the ten Liberal members will bestir themselves to expose the shortcomings of the government; consequently the task of ferreting out information will devolve upon the handful of Conservative and leftist members.
I am prefacing my remarks with this quotation because it will have a bearing upon what I have to say later on. I do not think it was the intention of this newspaper to cast any reflection upon any member of this
1272	COMMONS
War Expenditures-Special Committee
House of Commons. Is there not cause for the opinion expressed in this paper? Have not hon. members on the government side given the people of Canada the impression that they are nothing but what might be termed "yes" men? Rightly or wrongly, that is the impression given to the Canadian people. There is no doubt that all hon. members have a duty to support the government when they think it is right. But there is also a duty to criticize the government when they think it is wrong, more especially in times like these. That is the attitude I have taken. I have been impressed with the fact that Liberal members have not indicated any independence of mind in their criticism of the government. The hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount (Mr. Abbott) says that their hands are not tied. If that is so, why do they not rise in their places and criticize the government when they think it is wrong? What else can the public of this country or members of this house think but that they are just "yes" men?
I have heard hon. members of the opposition criticized severely because they had the audacity to differ with the government of the day. Some hon. members have been called saboteurs and accused of hindering Canada's war effort because they have criticized the government or have tried to obtain information which belongs rightly to the people of this country and to members of this house. We have our duty as members of this house, and I intend to carry out my duty.
There has been very little criticism on the part of Liberal members. I have listened to political harangues which have been made, not only by hon. members but by some ministers in an endeavour to discredit opposition members who have attempted to criticize the government.

There is no doubt in my mind that this committee can play a very useful part in the prosecution of our war effort. If the committee does not think that the powers given it are wide enough, it can come back to the house and ask for wider powers. As to sitting
[Mr. Douglas G. Rossd
in secret or in public, I think it should be left to the committee to decide when it is necessary to sit in camera. There will be a few times when it will be necessary for the committee to sit in camera, but on every possible occasion I think the meetings should be public. Any decision in this regard made by the committee should not be influenced in the slightest degree by politics. It may be difficult for hon. members to forsake their party politics in connection with this committee, but any effort to play politics there will be open to censure and should be made public to the country. Every hon. member who acts in this way should have to answer, not only to the public but to his own conscience.
Last evening the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) expressed himself quite forcibly. I agree with much of what he eaid, but I take exception to his remarks as reported on page 1248 of Hansard:
That, I believe, can be done by a thorough and careful inquiry writhout regard to publicity. We will not be concerned in the committee as to what the public thinks; we will be concerned with the knowledge within ourselves, as members of the committee, that we are doing an honest and thorough job of investigation.
A few moments ago the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount said that he could see no reason why any of the meetings of this committee should be held in public. The committee will certainly be concerned over this inquiry being an honest and thorough job of investigation, but it must also be concerned as to what the public thinks. One of the main reasons for the setting-up of this committee is that the public will get all the information. The usefulness of the committee will be lost unless the public are thoroughly informed, and suspicion will be cast upon the committee unless proper publicity is given to its labours. I do not mean publicity by way of propaganda; I mean real, honest publicity. The committee must be fearless.
I should like to express this hope, too, that the press of the country will be restrained in publishing reports and facts and criticisms brought out by the committee. If these points are kept in mind and a course such as I have outlined is followed I feel that a new wave of confidence will sweep over the public.
I wish now to say a word about the membership of the committee. I have in my hand the membership of the select committee on national expenditures of the British House of Commons, taken from page 1136 of the British Hansard of December 12, 1939, and I should

There was evidently a great desire on the part of the government there to ensure that there was a good representation of opposition members on that committee.
I should like to say one word more with respect to the composition of our own committee here. The degree of confidence which the public will have in our committee will be measured by the party representation from the House of Commons on the committee. Our committee is composed of twenty-four members-eighteen Liberals, four Conservatives, one Cooperative Commonwealth Federation member and one Social Credit member. There will probably be seven or eight subcommittees, and as the committee is at present constituted it is difficult to see how a representative of the opposition can be placed on
each of these subcommittees. I think public confidence in our party system would be greater if there were a larger representation of opposition members on this committee, regardless of the size of its representation in the house, and I commend that thought to the government. May I remind them that the opposition members of this House of Commons represent in the neighbourhood of 44 per cent of the people of Canada.
I have spoken on this resolution, Mr. Speaker, only because of the anxiety in my mind that the committee should be an outstanding success and of the greatest possible service both to the government and to the country in carrying on the war effort of Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall delay the
house for only a moment to make one or two observations which may be of some interest. Yesterday we adopted a resolution to appoint a committee to study the defence of Canada regulations. That committee follows the one which was set up last year, and in view of the discussion which has taken place to-day, the experience of the members of the committee which sat last year on the defence of Canada regulations may be of interest to the house. We met twenty-five times under the chairmanship of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). Many members have testified to the interest and pleasure of the work of that committee, and I subscribe to all that has been said in that regard, but no one so far has pointed out that during the whole sittings of that committee we did not have a single vote taken on a party basis. I would suggest that this example might well be followed in the committee that we are considering setting up to-day.
These two committees on war expenditure and the defence of Canada regulations, all members will agree, are designed to do some of the most important work of the house this session. The committee on the defence of Canada regulations, I suggest, may well follow along the lines of the concluding paragraph of the main part of the report of the committee last year, and may I observe to the hon. member for Weybum (Mr. Douglas) that that paragraph was unanimously agreed to. It read:
In making the recommendations for amendments to the regulations as above set forth and in considering amendments suggested but not included above, it was the unanimous view of the committee that all measures should be taken which were considered necessary for the safety of Canada but that the maximum amount of liberty under the law should be maintained consistent therewith.

War Expenditures-Special Committee
That was the principle on which our committee worked, and I think its report bears out my statement. I might add that the government, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) said, adopted without a single change eveiy conclusion and recommendation of that committee.
These committees will be valuable, only in so far as we approach their work in the spirit which has been so well described by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and all speakers, practically without exception, who have followed him. Our object in these committees is to strike at the enemy and not at each other.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The work of this committee has been delayed already much too long, far too many months, for us to wish to delay it any longer, even for five minutes. But there are a few points which I should like to make at this time.
First, I would draw the attention of the house to the enormous job which is facing this committee. Canada has been at war for well over a year and a half. The public accounts committee did not sit at all last year; I think the last time it met was when the Bren machine gun contract was under fire. Canada is paying the bill. The Canadian people have a right to know completely and thoroughly what is being done with the money, where it is being spent, and the types of contracts which are being let.
Going down the street the other day, I saw an exhibit of war material, indicating the prices which had been paid for parachutes and tommy guns. The people of Canada should have had that information a long time ago. The veil which has shrouded the details of expenditure has been left far too long. I hope that the committee will carry out its responsibility in seeing to it that this house and the whole of Canada know how this money is being spent.
Many people in the west are denying themselves necessities in order to buy war savings stamps-people who can ill afford to live on the lower standard which is now demanded of them; people who have very little left; some of them people who have been living on relief for a number of years. While making these sacrifices, they wish to know, and they have a right to know, what is being done with the money; how it is being spent, and where.
I hope that the committee will keep this house thoroughly informed.
I do not see how the committee can get through the pile of work which is ahead of them unless they sit continuously from now on, and if we take into account the other 
contracts which will be coming in-almost as long as the war lasts. Their work should be thorough; that much they owe to the Canadian people. Everything they find out should be placed without hesitancy before this house and the facts published to the Canadian people. As a democracy, we demand that everyone shall know what is happening.
Motion (Mr. Mackenzie King) agreed to.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-STATEMENT OF MR. SENN ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-STATEMENT OF MR. SENN ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Under our present system of responsible government as it exists in this country, it is the privilege-[DOT] the time-honoured privilege-of representatives of the people to ask for redress of their grievances and to discuss matters of public importance when parliament is being asked to vote supply. I intend, therefore, to bring to the attention of the house, and more particularly to the attention of the government, the plight in which our great primary industry of agriculture finds itself throughout the Dominion of Canada; and before I resume my seat-or at least before I conclude my remarks, because I see that the time from now until six o'clock is short-I intend to move an amendment to the motion which is now before the house.
That conditions surrounding agriculture in this country to-day are unsatisfactory needs no proof. Perhaps it is difficult for people who are not acquainted with farm life, and who see, as they do, the pleasant environment which surrounds agriculture in many parts of the country, to understand that agriculture is experiencing these difficulties. Mother Nature, in her bounty, has accorded ample opportunity to the farmers of this country to be prosperous and to live happy and contented lives. Living as we do in this northern zone, she has provided for us a climate which, though somewhat rigorous, is healthful and exhilarating and which for a good many months in the year is conducive to the growth and development of plant and animal life. Moreover, she has planted within Canada vast areas of the most fertile soil which can be found anywhere in the world, areas of soil which provide for the production of a great variety of crops, ranging all the way from hardy cereals to sub-tropical fruits and vegetables. Science and invention, on the other hand, have provided the equipment for the farmers of Canada whereby they can produce almost anything

Supply-State oj Agriculture
which can be produced anywhere in the world 

equipment in the line of implements of production, motor cars, radio, hydro appliances of different kinds, so that the farmers are in a very happy position even to the extent of comparing favourably with their city cousins.
The great difficulty which surrounds agriculture to-day can be sized up, I think, in one sentence. It is this, that the income or the revenue of the average farm in Canada is not sufficient to-day to provide for costs of production and at the same time to maintain a reasonable standard of living for the farmer and his family. During the past twenty-five years a great change has come over agriculture throughout the dominion. In the years just prior to the great war and all through the great war, farmers of Canada enjoyed a modicum of prosperity, which has completely vanished at the present time. During the years which have followed that time, they have found that their reserves have been largely dissipated, and land values in this country have dropped perhaps 50 per cent or more. Anybody driving through the country will readily see that the buildings, the fences, the equipment of the average farm are sadly in need of paint and of repair. Indeed, although I hesitate to say it, it is undoubtedly true that a very large proportion of the farmers of this country to-day are insolvent. Many others have their holdings heavily encumbered and are in an unfortunate way so far as their finances are concerned. The reason for that is not difficult to find. During the past twenty years farmers have found a great increase in their production costs, an increase in their labour costs, an increase in the cost of implements of production and a great increase in taxation, while during that period farm prices and farm revenues have not advanced to any degree and in many instances, have been reduced from what they were previously.
In proof of what I have been saying with regard to farm revenues, I would refer to a document which most hon. members will recognize by looking at it. It is part of what is known as the Sirois report. I am referring to appendix 4 dealing with national income. On page 59 I find some interesting figures. There we have a report of the net income of the farmers of Canada after allowing for depreciation of buildings and equipment. The years that are given are from 1926 to 1937, twelve years, and the national income for those twelve years amounted to $5,261,000,000, or an average, during those years, of $439,000,000 per annum. When we remember that in the last census it was shown that there are some 730,000 farmers in the dominion, it will be seen that the yearly income of the farmers
of Canada for those twelve years amounted to $600.50. Taking the first eight years of the depression, from 1930 to 1937, hon. members will find that the average income of the farmers was only $290,000,000, and dividing that among all the farmers of Canada, they will find that the yearly average income of the farmer was only $400.50.
Let me carry that further. That total amount of income for the twelve years, as given in this table, shows that the farmer received for those twelve years only 11-3 per cent of the total national income, and for the eight years I have mentioned he received only 8-67 per cent. Yet the farmers of the dominion represent between 35 and 40 per cent of the population.
I wish to go a step further. I find that the farmer is charged in this table, for income in kind for the house in which he has been living, $80 a year on the average; so that it will be found that, instead of receiving $600 on the average for that time, he had only, in cash, some $520, and for the eight years, $320. Why that was added to the farmer's income it is difficult for me to understand.
I think I have said enough and quoted sufficiently from this table to convince every hon. member present that the farmers have not been receiving a fair share of the national income. They have been trying all through the years to maintain a reasonable standard of living which would induce their families to stay on the farms, and in the attempt they have been dissipating their reserves until to-day they find themselves, in altogether too many instances, in a very unfortunate position indeed.
The outbreak of the great war brought many new problems to the dominion, and all these problems have only served to accentuate and bring into bolder relief the problems which agriculture is facing at the present time. The government of necessity has been forced to purchase huge quantities of war materials of all kinds, and has made contracts amounting in the past year to over three-quarters of a billion dollars. All these contracts, so far as I know, have been based on cost of production plus profit. In addition, the government has seen fit in its wisdom to ensure that labour will receive the same scale of wages as it received between the years 1927 and 1929, with the added provision that, if cost of living rises, wages will also rise. I want to make it abundantly clear that I am not finding fault with that. It was the only course the government could follow, and I am sure the farmers of Canada themselves would not say anything else; for the reason that they know that, if industry
Supply-State of Agriculture

and labour are prosperous, they will be ready and willing to buy more liberally of what the farmer produces.
On the other hand, the farmers cannot help feeling that an injustice has been done to them when war prices have to a certain extent set the prices of other industrial goods while farmers are not enjoying an equilibrium or a level of prices comparable with that enjoyed by industry and business. Indeed, the smouldering discontent under which, for some time past, farmers have been labouring, broke into open flame recently when they learned of the action of the war-time prices and trade board-which is of course a body created by this government-in pegging the price of butter. I think I am justified in making the statement that there is in the minds of farmers in many parts of the country a deep-seated resentment against the present administration. If anyone doubts that, let me say that I recently attended a meeting of farmers in the city of London gathered together to discuss prices, and I do not think I have ever seen a more hostile crowd than that faced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) at that time.
